formulas.name: Multiple regression forecast
formulas.vars: b_j = partial slope: change in Y per unit change in X_j holding the other X's constant; X_jf = assumed value of X_j for the forecast
formulas.use: Forecasts Y by plugging an assumed value of every independent variable into the estimated equation.
formulas.trap: Dropping statistically insignificant variables at forecast time; every variable in the estimated model must be plugged in.

formulas.name: t-test and confidence interval for a coefficient
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} t = \frac{\hat{b}_j - B_j}{s_{\hat{b}_j}} \\ \hat{b}_j \pm t_c\, s_{\hat{b}_j},\quad df = n-k-1 \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: B_j = hypothesized value (0 or e.g. 1 for beta); s = coefficient standard error; k = number of independent variables
formulas.use: Tests one slope against a hypothesized value or builds its confidence interval; zero outside the interval means reject b_j = 0.
formulas.trap: Using the printed t-stat (which tests B_j = 0) when the null is B_j = 1, or using n - 2 df instead of n - k - 1.

formulas.name: R² from the ANOVA table
formulas.vars: SST = RSS + SSE; RSS = regression (explained) sum of squares; SSE = sum of squared residuals e_i = Y_i - fitted Y_i
formulas.use: Gives the share of the variation in Y explained by all the regressors together, read straight from the ANOVA table.
formulas.trap: Swapping RSS (explained) and SSE (unexplained), or treating a higher R² as a better model: it never falls when a variable is added.

formulas.name: Adjusted R²
formulas.use: Compares models with the same dependent variable while penalizing extra regressors; it rises only if the new variable has |t| > 1.
formulas.trap: Reading adjusted R² as the percent of variation explained; it is always below R², can be negative, and can fall when R² rises.

formulas.name: Standard error of estimate (SEE)
formulas.use: Measures the typical size of the residuals in units of Y; a smaller SEE means a tighter in-sample fit.
formulas.trap: Dividing SSE by n or n - 1 instead of n - k - 1, or treating SEE as the full forecast error, which also has coefficient uncertainty.

formulas.name: Overall F-statistic
formulas.vars: H0: all slope coefficients = 0; df = k (numerator) and n - k - 1 (denominator)
formulas.use: Tests whether the regressors jointly explain any variation in Y; a one-tailed test where only large F rejects.
formulas.trap: Using a two-tailed critical value, or concluding that every slope is significant because the overall F rejects.

formulas.name: Joint F-test for q restrictions
formulas.vars: R = restricted (nested) model without the q tested variables; U = unrestricted model with all k variables; df = q and n - k - 1
formulas.use: Tests whether a subset of q variables can be dropped together by comparing the SSE of nested models.
formulas.trap: Dividing the SSE gap by k instead of q, putting SSE_R in the denominator, or taking df from the restricted model.

formulas.name: Akaike information criterion (AIC)
formulas.use: Ranks competing models fit to the same Y and sample when the goal is forecasting; the lowest AIC wins.
formulas.trap: Picking the model with the higher AIC; lower is better, and AIC (penalty 2 per parameter) is the forecasting criterion.

formulas.name: Bayesian information criterion (BIC)
formulas.use: Ranks competing models when the goal is goodness of fit; its heavier penalty favors more parsimonious models.
formulas.trap: Forgetting that ln(n) exceeds 2 once n > 7, so BIC penalizes extra parameters more than AIC in any realistic sample.

formulas.name: Omitted variable bias
formulas.vars: X_2 = omitted relevant variable with true slope b_2; bias sign = sign of b_2 times sign of Cov(X_1, X_2)
formulas.use: Shows how an included slope absorbs the effect of a correlated omitted variable and predicts the direction of the bias.
formulas.trap: Assuming a bigger sample removes the bias; omitted variable bias makes the slope inconsistent, not just imprecise.

formulas.name: Breusch–Pagan test statistic
formulas.vars: R²_resid = R² from regressing the squared residuals on the original k independent variables
formulas.use: Detects conditional heteroskedasticity; a one-tailed chi-square test that, if it rejects, calls for robust standard errors.
formulas.trap: Plugging in the R² of the original regression instead of the auxiliary residual regression, or using k - 1 df.

formulas.name: Durbin–Watson statistic
formulas.vars: r = first-order sample autocorrelation of residuals; DW near 2 = none, below 2 = positive, above 2 = negative serial correlation
formulas.use: Screens a regression for first-order serial correlation in the residuals when no lagged Y is a regressor.
formulas.trap: Running DW on an AR model or with lagged Y as a regressor; it is invalid there and tests only one lag, so use Breusch–Godfrey.

formulas.name: Breusch–Godfrey auxiliary regression
formulas.vars: H0: all p lag coefficients rho are zero, tested with an F-statistic with p and n - p - k - 1 df
formulas.use: Tests for serial correlation up to p lags; valid even when a lagged dependent variable is among the regressors.
formulas.trap: Fixing detected serial correlation by changing the coefficients; the remedy is Newey–West standard errors, slopes are unchanged.

formulas.name: Variance inflation factor (VIF)
formulas.vars: R²_j = R² from regressing X_j on all the other independent variables (not on Y); VIF > 5 investigate, > 10 serious
formulas.use: Quantifies multicollinearity for each regressor; high VIF explains a significant F-test with insignificant t-stats.
formulas.trap: Using the main regression's R² instead of X_j on the other X's, or saying multicollinearity biases slopes: it inflates their SEs.

formulas.name: Intercept and slope dummies
formulas.latex: Y_i = b_0 + d_0D_i + b_1X_i + d_1(D_i \times X_i) + \varepsilon_i
formulas.vars: D = 1 for the group, 0 for the base; d_0 = intercept shift; d_1 = slope shift. With m categories use m - 1 dummies
formulas.use: Lets a group have its own intercept and slope; a significant d_1 means the effect of X genuinely differs by group.
formulas.trap: Reading d_1 as the group's slope (the group slope is b_1 + d_1), or using m dummies plus an intercept (the dummy variable trap).

formulas.name: Leverage threshold
formulas.vars: h_ii = leverage of observation i, between 0 and 1: distance of its X values from the mean of the X's
formulas.use: Flags observations whose independent-variable values are extreme enough to pull the fitted regression.
formulas.trap: Confusing leverage (extreme X) with an outlier (extreme Y given X); high leverage alone does not prove influence.

formulas.name: Studentized residual
formulas.vars: e_i* = deleted residual: Y_i minus its prediction from the model estimated without observation i; s_e* = its standard deviation
formulas.use: Tests whether an observation is an outlier in Y by comparing |t*| with the critical t at n - k - 2 df.
formulas.trap: Spotting outliers with raw residuals; an influential point pulls the line toward itself and shrinks its own raw residual.

formulas.name: Cook's distance
formulas.vars: k = number of independent variables (curriculum form; general texts use k + 1 parameters). D_i > 0.5 may be, > 1 likely, > 2 sqrt(k/n) highly likely influential
formulas.use: Combines residual size and leverage to show whether deleting one observation shifts the fitted values materially.
formulas.trap: Treating a large residual or high leverage alone as proof of influence; Cook's D is large only when the two combine.

formulas.name: Logistic regression: log-odds and probability
formulas.vars: P/(1 - P) = odds; e^b_j = odds ratio, the multiplier on the odds per one-unit rise in X_j; estimated by maximum likelihood
formulas.use: Models a binary outcome such as default; convert the fitted log-odds to a probability between 0 and 1.
formulas.trap: Reading a slope as the change in probability per unit of X; it is the change in log-odds, so the probability effect varies.

formulas.name: Likelihood ratio test
formulas.vars: ln L = log-likelihood (negative; closer to 0 is a better fit); R = restricted model; q = number of restrictions
formulas.use: Tests the joint significance of logistic regression coefficients, the role the F-test plays in OLS.
formulas.trap: Applying an F-test or ordinary R² to a logistic model, or dropping the -2 so the statistic comes out negative.

formulas.name: Log-linear trend model
formulas.latex: \ln y_t = b_0 + b_1 t + \varepsilon_t,\qquad \hat{y}_t = e^{\hat{b}_0+\hat{b}_1 t}
formulas.vars: b_1 = continuously compounded growth per period (discrete rate = e^b_1 - 1); a linear trend y_t = b_0 + b_1 t grows by a constant amount
formulas.use: Fits a series that grows at a constant rate, such as sales; a linear trend leaves curved, serially correlated residuals.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to exponentiate the fitted log value when forecasting, or fitting a linear trend to constant-percentage growth.

formulas.name: AR(1) mean-reverting level and chain-rule forecast
formulas.vars: Requires |b_1| < 1 (covariance stationary); above the level the model forecasts a fall, below it a rise
formulas.use: Finds the level an AR(1) reverts to and builds multi-period forecasts by feeding each forecast back in as the lag.
formulas.trap: Computing b_0/(1 + b_1), or doubling the one-step change for two periods instead of chaining; with b_1 = 1 the level is undefined.

formulas.name: t-test on residual autocorrelation
formulas.vars: rho_e,k = residual autocorrelation at lag k; T = number of observations
formulas.use: Checks an AR model for serially correlated residuals lag by lag, since Durbin–Watson is invalid for AR models.
formulas.trap: Using 1/T instead of 1/sqrt(T) as the standard error; any significant lag means adding lags to the model.

formulas.name: Random walk and first differencing
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} x_t = b_0 + x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \\ y_t = x_t - x_{t-1} = b_0 + \varepsilon_t \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: b_0 = drift (0 for a pure random walk); a random walk is an AR(1) with b_1 = 1, a unit root
formulas.use: Turns a unit-root series, whose variance grows without bound, into a stationary series that can be modeled.
formulas.trap: Modeling the levels of a random walk with AR and trusting the t-stats; its mean-reverting level b_0/(1 - b_1) does not exist.

formulas.name: Dickey–Fuller unit root test
formulas.vars: H0: g_1 = 0 (unit root) vs Ha: g_1 < 0 (stationary); the t-stat on g_1 uses Dickey–Fuller critical values
formulas.use: Tests a series for a unit root before using it in an AR model or a regression with another time series.
formulas.trap: Using ordinary t critical values, which are too small in absolute value, or reversing H0: the null is that a unit root exists.

formulas.name: Seasonal lag in an AR model
formulas.vars: x_t-4 = same quarter last year (use x_t-12 for monthly data)
formulas.use: Captures seasonality flagged by a significant residual autocorrelation at the seasonal lag (4 quarterly, 12 monthly).
formulas.trap: Ignoring a lag-4 spike because lags 1-3 look clean, or forecasting without the same-quarter-last-year value.

formulas.name: ARCH(1) test and variance forecast
formulas.vars: A significant a_1 means ARCH: error variance depends on last period's squared error (volatility clusters)
formulas.use: Tests a time-series model for volatility clustering and, if present, forecasts next period's error variance.
formulas.trap: Regressing raw rather than squared residuals on their lag; that tests serial correlation, not ARCH.

formulas.name: Out-of-sample RMSE
formulas.vars: n = number of holdout observations not used in estimation
formulas.use: Compares forecasting models on holdout data; the model with the lowest out-of-sample RMSE forecasts best.
formulas.trap: Choosing the model with the best in-sample R² or SEE; in-sample fit rewards capturing noise, not forecasting accuracy.

formulas.name: LASSO objective
formulas.vars: lambda = penalty hyperparameter set by the researcher, usually by cross-validation; lambda = 0 gives OLS
formulas.use: Shrinks coefficients and sets some exactly to zero, selecting features and curbing overfitting with many correlated regressors.
formulas.trap: Treating lambda as a coefficient estimated from the data; it is a hyperparameter, and a larger lambda keeps fewer variables.

formulas.name: PCA share of variance explained
formulas.vars: lambda_j = eigenvalue of principal component j (here not the LASSO penalty); p = number of original features
formulas.use: Decides how many principal components to keep, typically enough to explain about 85-95% of total variance.
formulas.trap: Labeling a component as one original variable; each is a weighted blend, and PCA ignores Y, so top components need not predict best.

formulas.name: Normalization and standardization
formulas.use: Puts features on a common scale before training; normalization maps to 0-1, standardization centers on mean 0, SD 1.
formulas.trap: Normalizing a feature with large outliers, which squashes the other values; standardization is less sensitive to outliers.

formulas.name: TF-IDF
formulas.vars: TF = token count in a sentence / tokens in that sentence; DF = sentences containing the token / total sentences; IDF = log(1/DF), base only rescales
formulas.use: Weights tokens for text features: frequent within a document but rare across documents scores highest.
formulas.trap: Ranking by raw frequency; a token in every document has DF = 1, so IDF = 0 and it carries no discriminating power.

formulas.name: Precision
formulas.vars: TP = true positives; FP = false positives (Type I errors)
formulas.use: Share of predicted positives that are correct; the metric to watch when false positives are costly.
formulas.trap: Swapping precision and recall: precision divides by predicted positives (TP + FP), not actual positives.

formulas.name: Recall
formulas.vars: FN = false negatives (Type II errors), e.g. defaults the model missed; also called sensitivity
formulas.use: Share of actual positives the model catches; the metric to watch when missing a positive, such as a default, is costly.
formulas.trap: Dividing by predicted positives instead of actual positives (TP + FN), which turns recall into precision.

formulas.name: Accuracy
formulas.use: Share of all classifications that are correct; meaningful only when the classes are of similar size.
formulas.trap: Praising high accuracy on imbalanced data: if 95% of bonds never default, predicting no default for all scores 95%.

formulas.name: F1 score
formulas.vars: P = precision; R = recall; F1 is their harmonic mean
formulas.use: Single score balancing precision and recall; preferred over accuracy when classes are unequal in size.
formulas.trap: Averaging precision and recall arithmetically; the harmonic mean is pulled toward the weaker of the two.

definitions.def: Linearity, homoskedastic errors, no serial correlation, normally distributed errors (for small-sample tests) and no exact linear relation among the X's. Normality applies to the error term, not to the X variables.

Error variance that is correlated with the independent variables. Slopes stay unbiased, but standard errors are usually understated, inflating t-stats. Unconditional heteroskedasticity causes no major problem.

White (heteroskedasticity-consistent) SEs fix inference under conditional heteroskedasticity; Newey–West SEs also fix serial correlation. Both change standard errors and t-stats, never the coefficients.
Omitting a variable, using the wrong form (e.g. size instead of ln size, fixed by a log-log model), wrong scaling, or pooling data from different regimes. Robust SEs cannot repair biased slopes.

Positive serial correlation leaves slopes consistent but understates standard errors, inflating t and F. If a lagged dependent variable is a regressor, the coefficients themselves become inconsistent.
A point whose removal materially changes the slopes, their significance or R². It usually combines high leverage (extreme X) with a large residual (outlier in Y); check Cook's D before deleting.
Constant, finite mean and variance and constant covariance at each lag through time. AR(p) estimates and t-tests are valid only for stationary series; trends, random walks and breaks violate it.
Two unit-root series share a long-run link, so residuals from regressing one on the other are stationary (Engle–Granger test). Then the regression is valid; without it, it is spurious.
Out-of-sample error = bias error (underfitting) + variance error (overfitting) + base error (noise). An overfit model has low bias but high variance error; reduce complexity or regularize.
Supervised learning uses labeled targets: regression for continuous Y, classification for categorical Y. Unsupervised learning has no target and finds structure via PCA or clustering.

A tree of binary splits, each chosen to minimize impurity such as Gini = 1 - sum of squared class shares (or squared error for regression). Captures nonlinearity; limit depth or prune to avoid overfit.
Shuffle data into k parts, train on k - 1 and validate on the remaining part, rotating k times; the average validation error estimates out-of-sample error and tunes hyperparameters.
An ensemble of trees, each fit on a bootstrap sample with a random subset of features at each split; majority vote or averaging lowers variance error at the cost of interpretability.

K-means needs k up front and reassigns points to the nearest centroid until stable. Hierarchical clustering needs no k: agglomerative merges bottom-up, divisive splits top-down, shown as a dendrogram.
Trimming removes extreme observations from the data set; winsorization keeps them but replaces extreme values with cutoff values such as the 1st and 99th percentiles.
Both normalize tokens in text preparation. Stemming crudely cuts to a root ('increasing' to 'increas'); lemmatization returns the dictionary base form ('better' to 'good') at higher compute cost.

drill.why: Scaling (1 - R²) by the degrees-of-freedom ratio (n - 1)/(n - k - 1) penalizes extra regressors: that is adjusted R². Plain R² has no df ratio, and VIF also uses 1 - R² but inverts it, with R² from X_j on the other X's.

Two SSEs from nested models and division by q restrictions mark the joint F-test. The overall F uses RSS/k over SSE/(n - k - 1) from one model; the likelihood ratio test compares log-likelihoods, not SSEs.
A penalty of 2 per parameter on n ln(SSE/n) is AIC, the forecasting criterion. BIC has the same first term but penalizes ln(n) per parameter, which is heavier for n > 7 and favors smaller models.

n times the R² of squared residuals regressed on the X's, chi-square with k df, is Breusch–Pagan for conditional heteroskedasticity. The likelihood ratio test is also chi-square but uses -2 times a log-likelihood gap.

One over (1 - R²_j), with R²_j from regressing X_j on the other regressors, is the variance inflation factor for multicollinearity. Adjusted R² also contains 1 - R² but multiplies it by a df ratio and subtracts from 1.

Squared residual times a leverage term h/(1 - h)² combines both sources of influence: Cook's distance. The leverage threshold uses h_ii alone, and the studentized residual uses only the deleted residual.

distractors: Seasonal lag in an AR model
drill.why: Intercept over (1 - b_1) is the AR(1) mean-reverting level, defined only when |b_1| < 1. In a random walk b_1 = 1, so this ratio is undefined; Dickey–Fuller tests b_1 - 1 rather than dividing by it.

distractors: AR(1) mean-reverting level and chain-rule forecast
drill.why: Regressing the change in x on the lagged level and testing g_1 = b_1 - 1 = 0 is the Dickey–Fuller unit root test. First differencing also uses the change in x, but with no lagged level; it is the remedy, not the test.

True positives over all predicted positives (TP + FP) is precision. Recall has the same numerator but divides by actual positives (TP + FN); accuracy adds TN to the numerator and uses all four cells below.

Squared residuals regressed on their own lag is the ARCH(1) test. Breusch–Godfrey regresses raw residuals on lagged raw residuals (serial correlation); Breusch–Pagan regresses squared residuals on the X's, not on their lag.

formulas.name: Bid–offer cross rate
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} S^{bid}_{A/C} = S^{bid}_{A/B} \times S^{bid}_{B/C} \\ S^{offer}_{A/C} = S^{offer}_{A/B} \times S^{offer}_{B/C} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: A/B = units of A per one unit of base currency B. To invert a leg: new bid = 1/old offer, new offer = 1/old bid
formulas.use: Derives a cross-rate quote from two legs that share an intermediate currency, keeping the dealer's spread on both sides.
formulas.trap: Inverting a leg with 1/bid as the new bid, or multiplying a bid by an offer; a cross spread narrower than the legs signals the error.

formulas.name: Covered interest rate parity forward rate
formulas.vars: P = price currency; B = base currency; i = money-market rates quoted on an actual/360 basis
formulas.use: Prices an FX forward by no-arbitrage from spot and the two money-market rates over the contract term.
formulas.trap: Putting the base-currency rate in the numerator, or using annual rates without the days/360 scaling.

formulas.name: Forward premium or discount (forward points)
formulas.vars: Forward points = (F - S) x 10,000 for four-decimal pairs; F > S means the base currency trades at a forward premium
formulas.use: Gives the forward premium or discount directly; the lower-yielding base currency trades at a forward premium.
formulas.trap: Reading a forward discount on the high-yield currency as an expected depreciation; that needs uncovered parity, not covered.

formulas.name: Mark-to-market value of an FX forward
formulas.vars: F_t = forward rate now for an offsetting contract with the same settlement date; days = days remaining; V in price currency, + for long base
formulas.use: Values an existing forward before settlement: lock in the gain with an offsetting forward and discount it to today.
formulas.trap: Discounting at the base-currency rate or over the original term; the gain is in the price currency and uses days remaining.

formulas.name: Covered interest arbitrage profit
formulas.vars: Per 1 unit of price currency borrowed for one period; a positive value means borrow P, buy B spot, invest at i_B, sell B forward
formulas.use: Measures the riskless gain when a dealer's forward quote departs from the covered-parity forward rate.
formulas.trap: Trading in the wrong direction: always sell forward the currency whose forward is overpriced versus parity; reverse every leg if negative.

formulas.name: Uncovered interest rate parity
formulas.vars: Exact form: E(S_T)/S = (1 + i_P)/(1 + i_B); a rise in S_P/B means the base currency appreciates
formulas.use: Gives the spot change that equalizes expected returns: the high-yield currency is expected to depreciate by its yield edge.
formulas.trap: Treating UIP as an arbitrage condition (only covered parity is), or flipping the sign so the high-yield currency appreciates.

formulas.name: Absolute PPP
formulas.vars: P_P, P_B = price of the same basket in the price-currency and base-currency countries
formulas.use: Sets the long-run fair value of a currency; the gap between spot and the PPP rate is a slow valuation signal.
formulas.trap: Expecting the PPP gap to close within a year; transport costs, tariffs and non-tradables keep deviations alive for years.

formulas.name: Relative PPP
formulas.vars: pi = annual inflation; T = years. Approximation: %change in S_P/B is about pi_P - pi_B; ex ante PPP uses expected inflation pi^e for the expected spot
formulas.use: Forecasts the spot rate from the inflation gap: the higher-inflation currency depreciates and the real rate stays constant.
formulas.trap: Putting base-currency inflation in the numerator, or using the simple inflation gap instead of the ratio when inflation is high.

formulas.name: International Fisher effect and real rate parity
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} r_P - r_B \approx (i_P - i_B) - (\pi^e_P - \pi^e_B) \\ i_P - i_B \approx \pi^e_P - \pi^e_B \;\text{ if } r_P = r_B \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: r = real rate; i = nominal rate; pi^e = expected inflation. Real rate parity (r_P = r_B) follows from UIP plus ex ante PPP
formulas.use: Checks whether a nominal rate gap reflects only an inflation gap or a genuine real return advantage.
formulas.trap: Calling a high-nominal-rate currency attractive without checking real rates; the Fisher effect assumes equal real rates.

formulas.name: International parity chain
formulas.vars: Links covered parity, the Fisher effect, ex ante PPP and uncovered parity (E(S_T) = expected future spot)
formulas.use: When all parities hold, the forward rate is an unbiased forecast of the future spot and no currency earns excess return.
formulas.trap: Assuming the forward predicts the future spot whenever covered parity holds; unbiasedness also needs uncovered parity.

formulas.name: Real exchange rate
formulas.vars: A rise in q = real appreciation of the base currency. Approximation: %change in q is about %change in S_P/B + pi_B - pi_P
formulas.use: Adjusts the nominal rate for relative price levels to judge changes in competitiveness.
formulas.trap: Inverting the CPI ratio: with S quoted P/B, multiply by base-country CPI over price-country CPI.

formulas.name: Real exchange rate and real rate differentials
formulas.vars: q-bar = long-run equilibrium real rate; r = real interest rate; phi = risk premium
formulas.use: Explains short-run deviations: a currency with a higher real rate or lower risk premium trades above its long-run real value.
formulas.trap: Flipping the sign: a higher base-country risk premium lowers q (weaker base currency), while a higher base real rate raises it.

formulas.name: FX carry trade return
formulas.vars: H = high-yield investment currency; L = low-yield funding currency; S_L/H rises when the investment currency appreciates
formulas.use: Computes the funding-currency return on borrowing the low-yield currency and investing in the high-yield one.
formulas.trap: Calling carry an arbitrage; it profits only when uncovered parity fails and loses when the funding currency spikes.

formulas.name: Monetary approach: quantity theory
formulas.latex: MV = PY \;\Rightarrow\; \%\Delta P \approx \%\Delta M + \%\Delta V - \%\Delta Y
formulas.vars: M = money supply; V = velocity; P = price level; Y = real output
formulas.use: Long-run link from money growth to inflation; through PPP, faster money growth means proportional depreciation.
formulas.trap: Using it for the short-run path; with sticky prices the currency first overshoots its long-run level (Dornbusch).

formulas.name: Growth accounting (Cobb–Douglas)
formulas.vars: A = total factor productivity (TFP); alpha = capital's share of income; K = capital; L = labor
formulas.use: Splits GDP growth into TFP, capital and labor contributions; TFP growth is the residual after factor contributions.
formulas.trap: Weighting labor by alpha and capital by 1 - alpha, or treating TFP as measured directly; it is a residual.

formulas.name: Labor productivity growth
formulas.vars: K/L = capital per worker; alpha times its growth = capital deepening contribution
formulas.use: Separates output-per-worker growth into TFP and capital deepening, the part that fades with diminishing returns.
formulas.trap: Assuming capital deepening sustains growth forever; diminishing returns mean only TFP growth lifts long-run productivity.

formulas.name: Potential GDP growth
formulas.vars: Labor input = labor force growth (population, participation, net immigration) adjusted for change in average hours
formulas.use: Estimates sustainable GDP growth as the growth of labor input plus the growth of output per hour or per worker.
formulas.trap: Counting a cyclical fall in unemployment as higher potential growth, or ignoring falling average hours per worker.

formulas.name: Solow steady-state growth and output–capital ratio
formulas.vars: theta = TFP growth; alpha = capital's share; n = labor force growth; s = saving rate; delta = depreciation. Capital per worker grows at theta/(1 - alpha)
formulas.use: Gives steady-state growth of output per worker and of total output, and the constant output–capital ratio that saving sustains.
formulas.trap: Using theta alone for per-worker growth, or claiming a higher saving rate raises steady-state growth; it only lowers Y/K and lifts the level.

formulas.name: Endogenous (AK) growth rate
formulas.latex: y = f\,k \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\Delta y}{y} = \frac{\Delta k}{k} = s f - \delta - n
formulas.vars: y, k = output and capital per worker; f = constant marginal product of capital; s = saving rate; delta = depreciation
formulas.use: Shows how constant economy-wide returns to capital let a higher saving rate raise growth permanently.
formulas.trap: Applying diminishing returns to aggregate capital here; spillovers keep returns constant, so there is no steady state.

formulas.name: Equity market value and nominal GDP
formulas.vars: GDP is nominal (real potential growth plus inflation); E/GDP = earnings share of GDP
formulas.use: Ties long-run aggregate equity growth to nominal GDP growth, since the earnings share and P/E cannot rise forever.
formulas.trap: Extrapolating rising margins or multiples into perpetuity; only nominal GDP growth is sustainable for aggregate value.

definitions.term: Covered vs uncovered interest rate parity
definitions.def: Covered parity is a no-arbitrage condition using a forward contract and holds closely. Uncovered parity has no hedge, assumes risk neutrality and often fails in the short run, which carry trades exploit.

High capital mobility: tight money plus loose fiscal clearly appreciates the currency; loose money plus tight fiscal clearly depreciates it. Low mobility: fiscal expansion depreciates via the trade deficit.
With sticky goods prices, a surprise monetary expansion makes the currency fall more in the short run than its long-run PPP level, then recover as prices adjust. The long-run move is proportional.
Persistent fiscal deficits raise the supply of a country's bonds; investors hold them only at higher expected returns, so the initial Mundell–Fleming appreciation can reverse into depreciation.
Carry returns are negatively skewed with fat left tails: in risk-off episodes funding currencies such as JPY spike. Managers cut exposure as implied FX volatility and risk indicators rise.

Intervention works only if large relative to market turnover, so it is more effective in emerging markets. Temporary capital controls can be justified to stem hot-money inflows or disorderly outflows.

Real exchange rate well above trend, rapid credit growth, falling reserves versus short-term debt, a widening current account deficit and a peg. Risk peaks when several coincide, not on one indicator.

Absolute: all countries reach the same output per capita. Conditional: only countries with the same saving, population growth and technology converge. Club: poor countries converge only by joining via reform.
Investment = private saving + government saving (T - G) + foreign saving (M - X). Investment financed by foreign saving supplements domestic capital but leaves an economy exposed to sudden stops.

Neoclassical (Solow): diminishing returns to capital, exogenous TFP, saving changes only the level of output. Endogenous: R&D and human capital spillovers keep returns constant, so saving can raise growth permanently.
Capture: the regulator ends up serving the industry it oversees. Arbitrage: firms exploit gaps or differences between regulators or jurisdictions to avoid a rule's intent without breaking it.

Regulation targets informational frictions (adverse selection, moral hazard) and externalities. Tools: price mechanisms (taxes, subsidies), restrictions or requirements on activities, and public provision.

drill.why: Spot scaled by a ratio of money-market growth factors with days/360 is the covered parity forward rate. Relative PPP uses the same ratio shape but with inflation rates and gives an expected spot, not a forward price.

distractors: Covered interest rate parity forward rate
drill.why: A ratio of one-plus-inflation rates compounded over T years gives the expected spot change: relative PPP. Absolute PPP divides price levels, not inflation rates, and the CIP forward uses interest rates.

distractors: Real exchange rate and real rate differentials
drill.why: The nominal rate multiplied by base-country over price-country price levels is the real exchange rate. Absolute PPP sets the nominal rate equal to a price-level ratio rather than adjusting an observed spot rate by one.

distractors: Real exchange rate and real rate differentials
drill.why: An expected spot change equal to the nominal interest gap alone is uncovered parity. Relative PPP uses the inflation gap; carry return adds the spot change to the gap; the real-rate model uses real rates and risk premia.

distractors: Solow steady-state growth and output–capital ratio
drill.why: TFP growth plus share-weighted capital and labor growth adds up to total output growth: growth accounting. Labor productivity growth drops the labor term and uses growth in capital per worker instead of capital.

TFP growth scaled by 1/(1 - alpha) plus labor force growth n is steady-state total output growth in the Solow model. The AK model instead depends on the saving rate (sf - delta - n), with no steady state.

formulas.name: Equity method investment carrying value
formulas.latex: Inv_{end} = Inv_{beg} + (s \times NI_{assoc} - Amort) - s \times Div_{assoc}
formulas.vars: s = ownership share; Amort = investor's amortization of excess purchase price on step-ups; Div = dividends declared by the associate
formulas.use: Tracks the single-line investment asset for a 20–50% significant-influence stake across a reporting period.
formulas.trap: Booking the share of dividends as income; under the equity method dividends reduce the carrying value as a return of capital.

formulas.name: Equity income with excess purchase price amortization
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{Equity income} = s \times NI_{assoc} - Amort \\ Amort = \frac{s \times (FV - BV)_{\text{dep. assets}}}{\text{Remaining life}} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Excess = cost − s × BV of associate; allocate it first to assets with FV > BV, and the residual is goodwill, which is not amortized
formulas.use: Computes the income the investor reports when it paid more than its share of the associate's book value.
formulas.trap: Amortizing the goodwill residual, or amortizing 100% of an asset step-up instead of only the investor's share s of it.

formulas.name: Unrealized intercompany profit (equity method)
formulas.vars: Profit = total profit on the intercompany sale; units unsold = goods still held by the buyer at period end
formulas.use: Removes the investor's share of profit on upstream or downstream sales that are still in inventory at period end.
formulas.trap: Eliminating 100% of the profit (consolidation treatment) or only upstream sales; both directions eliminate share s.

formulas.name: Goodwill and bargain purchase gain
formulas.vars: FV_INA = fair value of identifiable net assets, including intangibles the target never recorded; the gain arises only when FV_INA is larger
formulas.use: Measures goodwill under the acquisition method, or the immediate P&L gain when the price is below the fair value of net assets.
formulas.trap: Recording negative goodwill as a liability or amortizing it; after reassessing fair values the excess is an immediate gain.

formulas.name: Full vs partial goodwill
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} GW_{full} = FV_{target,\,100\%} - FV_{INA} \\ GW_{partial} = \text{Price} - s \times FV_{INA} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: FV_target,100% = fair value of the whole target; s = acquirer's ownership share; FV_INA = fair value of identifiable net assets
formulas.use: Compares goodwill when NCI is measured at fair value (full) versus at its share of identifiable net assets (partial).
formulas.trap: Thinking US GAAP allows partial goodwill; US GAAP requires full goodwill, while IFRS lets the acquirer choose either.

formulas.name: Noncontrolling interest at acquisition
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} NCI_{full} = (1 - s) \times FV_{target,\,100\%} \\ NCI_{partial} = (1 - s) \times FV_{INA} \end{gathered}
formulas.use: Sets the NCI line in consolidated equity at acquisition; the method choice also moves total assets, equity and ROE.
formulas.trap: Using the target's book value; full NCI is larger, so the full method gives higher assets and equity and a lower ROE.

formulas.name: Goodwill impairment loss: IFRS vs US GAAP
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} Loss_{IFRS} = CV_{CGU} - \text{Recoverable amount} \\ Loss_{US} = \min(CV_{RU} - FV_{RU},\ GW) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Recoverable amount = higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use; CGU = cash-generating unit; RU = reporting unit
formulas.use: Sizes the write-down when a CGU or reporting unit is carried above its recoverable amount (IFRS) or fair value (US GAAP).
formulas.trap: Using the removed US GAAP two-step implied-goodwill test, or reversing a goodwill impairment; neither standard allows reversal.

formulas.name: PBO roll-forward
formulas.latex: PBO_{end} = PBO_{beg} + SC + r \times PBO_{beg} + PSC + AL - B
formulas.vars: SC = current service cost; r = discount rate; PSC = past service cost from amendments; AL = actuarial loss (negative if a gain); B = benefits paid
formulas.use: Reconciles the defined benefit obligation over a year and backs out a missing service cost or actuarial loss.
formulas.trap: Using the expected return on assets instead of the discount rate for interest cost, or reducing the PBO by contributions.

formulas.name: Plan assets roll-forward and funded status
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} FVPA_{end} = FVPA_{beg} + R_{actual} + C - B \\ FS = FVPA - PBO \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: R_actual = actual return on plan assets; C = employer contributions; B = benefits paid (reduce both assets and PBO); FS < 0 = net liability
formulas.use: Rolls plan assets forward and nets them against the PBO to get the single net pension asset or liability reported.
formulas.trap: Using the expected instead of the actual return, or forgetting the IFRS asset ceiling that caps a net asset when overfunded.

formulas.name: Total periodic pension cost (TPPC)
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} TPPC = PBO_{end} - PBO_{beg} + B - R_{actual} \\ TPPC = C - (FS_{end} - FS_{beg}) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Equals SC + interest cost + PSC + actuarial loss − actual return; identical under IFRS and US GAAP, only the P&L vs OCI split differs
formulas.use: Measures the full economic pension cost for the year, independent of how each standard splits it between P&L and OCI.
formulas.trap: Using the expected return, or treating TPPC as the P&L pension expense; the difference between the two sits in OCI.

formulas.name: Pension cost in P&L: IFRS vs US GAAP
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} P\&L_{IFRS} = SC + PSC + r\,(PBO_{beg} - FVPA_{beg}) \\ P\&L_{US} = SC + r\,PBO_{beg} - E(R)\,FVPA_{beg} + Amort \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: r = discount rate; E(R) = expected return on plan assets; Amort = amortization of past service cost and of actuarial losses beyond the corridor
formulas.use: Splits periodic pension cost into its P&L piece; IFRS remeasurements and unamortized US GAAP items go to OCI.
formulas.trap: Applying an expected return under IFRS; IAS 19 earns only the discount rate on assets, so a high return assumption helps US GAAP only.

formulas.name: US GAAP corridor amortization of actuarial losses
formulas.vars: NAL_beg = net actuarial loss (or gain, in absolute value) accumulated in AOCI at the start of the year; an amortized gain reduces expense
formulas.use: Computes the minimum actuarial loss or gain recycled from AOCI into US GAAP pension expense for the year.
formulas.trap: Using 10% of the smaller of PBO and plan assets, or amortizing the whole AOCI balance rather than the excess over the corridor.

formulas.name: CFO adjustment for contributions vs TPPC
formulas.vars: C = employer contributions; t = tax rate; a positive result is added back to CFO and treated as a financing outflow, like repaying debt
formulas.use: Reclassifies the after-tax excess (or shortfall) of employer contributions over TPPC from operating to financing cash flow.
formulas.trap: Adding back the pre-tax excess, or comparing contributions with P&L pension expense instead of TPPC, which includes OCI items.

formulas.name: Equity-settled share-based compensation expense
formulas.vars: FV_grant = grant-date fair value per award (option-pricing model for options, share price for restricted stock)
formulas.use: Spreads the grant-date fair value of options or restricted stock evenly over the service (vesting) period.
formulas.trap: Remeasuring equity-settled awards at each year-end; only cash-settled awards such as SARs are remeasured until settlement.

formulas.name: Cumulative translation adjustment (current rate)
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} CTA = NA_{LC} \times S_{end} - (Stock \times S_{hist} + RE_{\$}) \\ \Delta CTA \approx NA_{LC} \times (S_{end} - S_{beg}) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: S = parent currency per LC; NA_LC = net assets (the exposure); RE_$ = beginning translated RE + NI at average rate − dividends at declaration rate
formulas.use: Plugs the translated balance sheet when the LC is functional; the CTA sits in OCI and is recycled only on disposal of the sub.
formulas.trap: Putting the translation gain in net income (that is temporal remeasurement) or translating retained earnings at the current rate.

formulas.name: Remeasurement gain or loss (temporal method)
formulas.vars: NMP = net monetary position: monetary assets (plus items at current value) − monetary liabilities; negative = net monetary liability
formulas.use: Estimates the FX gain or loss in net income when the parent currency is functional or US GAAP sees a hyperinflationary sub.
formulas.trap: Using net assets as the exposure; with a net monetary liability a falling LC gives a gain while the current rate method shows a loss.

formulas.name: IAS 29 hyperinflation restatement
formulas.vars: Index = general price index; only non-monetary and income statement items are restated; NML = net monetary liability (a net monetary asset gives a loss)
formulas.use: Restates a hyperinflationary sub's LC statements under IFRS before translating every item at the current rate.
formulas.trap: Restating monetary items, or applying IAS 29 under US GAAP, which instead remeasures the sub with the temporal method.

formulas.name: Translated ROA under the current rate method
formulas.use: Shows how mixed ratios move when net income is translated at the average rate and assets at the year-end rate.
formulas.trap: Assuming all ratios survive translation; margins do, but with an appreciating LC (S_end > S_avg) translated ROA falls below LC ROA.

formulas.name: CET1 ratio and risk-weighted assets
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} CET1\ ratio = \frac{\text{Common equity} - \text{Deductions}}{RWA} \\ RWA = \textstyle\sum_i w_i \times EAD_i \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Deductions = goodwill, intangibles, certain DTAs; w = risk weight; EAD = exposure at default; RWA also adds market and operational risk charges
formulas.use: Measures the highest-quality loss-absorbing capital per unit of risk; headroom over 4.5% + 2.5% buffer shows payout capacity.
formulas.trap: Dividing by total assets instead of RWA, or leaving goodwill and intangibles in CET1; they are deducted first.

formulas.name: Tier 1 and total capital ratios
formulas.vars: AT1 = perpetual loss-absorbing instruments (CoCos, non-cumulative preferred); Tier 2 = subordinated debt and some allowances; minimums 6% and 8%
formulas.use: Checks Basel III minimums for going-concern (Tier 1) and gone-concern (Tier 2) capital against risk-weighted assets.
formulas.trap: Counting Tier 2 subordinated debt as going-concern capital; only CET1 and AT1 absorb losses while the bank operates.

formulas.name: Basel III leverage ratio
formulas.vars: Total exposure = on-balance-sheet assets + derivatives + securities financing + off-balance-sheet items, with no risk weighting
formulas.use: A non-risk-based backstop that caps balance-sheet size relative to Tier 1 capital, whatever the risk weights.
formulas.trap: Putting RWA or CET1 into this ratio; it is Tier 1 over unweighted exposure, so low risk weights cannot flatter it.

formulas.name: Liquidity coverage ratio (LCR)
formulas.vars: HQLA = high-quality liquid assets after haircuts; flows are stressed cash flows over the next 30 days
formulas.use: Tests whether high-quality liquid assets cover stressed net cash outflows over a 30-day stress horizon.
formulas.trap: Netting inflows in full; inflows are capped at 75% of outflows, so net outflows are at least 25% of gross outflows.

formulas.name: Net stable funding ratio (NSFR)
formulas.vars: ASF = available stable funding factor (capital 100%, stable retail deposits about 90–95%); RSF = required stable funding factor by asset
formulas.use: Tests structural funding over one year: stable liabilities and capital must cover assets that need stable funding.
formulas.trap: Confusing it with the LCR (30-day stress, HQLA over outflows); the NSFR weighs funding against assets over one year.

formulas.name: Insurer combined ratio
formulas.latex: \text{Combined} = \frac{\text{Losses} + LAE}{\text{Net premiums earned}} + \frac{\text{Underwriting exp.}}{\text{Net premiums written}}
formulas.vars: LAE = loss-adjustment expenses; loss and LAE ratio on premiums earned + underwriting expense ratio on premiums written (trade basis)
formulas.use: Measures P&C underwriting profitability before investment income; below 100% means an underwriting profit.
formulas.trap: Reading a combined ratio above 100% as an overall loss; investment income can still make the insurer profitable.

formulas.name: Accruals ratio: balance-sheet and cash-flow
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} AR^{BS} = \frac{NOA_{end} - NOA_{beg}}{(NOA_{end} + NOA_{beg})/2} \\ AR^{CF} = \frac{NI - (CFO + CFI)}{(NOA_{end} + NOA_{beg})/2} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: NOA = (total assets − cash and investments) − (total liabilities − total debt)
formulas.use: Scales aggregate accruals by average net operating assets; a higher ratio means a larger non-cash share of earnings.
formulas.trap: Leaving CFI out of the cash-flow version or scaling by total assets; both versions divide by average NOA.

formulas.name: Beneish M-score
formulas.vars: AQI asset quality, SGI sales growth, SGAI SG&A, LEVI leverage: year t vs t−1 indices; Accruals (TATA) = (income before extraordinary items − CFO) / total assets
formulas.use: Turns eight year-over-year indices into a probit score of earnings manipulation; scores above −1.78 flag likely manipulators.
formulas.trap: Reading a higher (less negative) M-score as safer; it means a higher manipulation probability, and it screens rather than proves.

formulas.name: Beneish DSRI, GMI and DEPI indices
formulas.vars: AR = receivables; GM = gross profit / sales; DR = depreciation rate = Dep / (Dep + PP&E)
formulas.use: M-score inputs: receivables outpacing sales (DSRI > 1), a falling gross margin (GMI > 1) or slower depreciation (DEPI > 1) raise it.
formulas.trap: Inverting GMI as GM_t / GM_t−1; the prior-year margin is on top, so a falling margin gives GMI > 1 and a higher score.

formulas.name: Earnings persistence regression
formulas.vars: CF_t = cash component of earnings; Accruals_t = accrual component; beta = persistence coefficient
formulas.use: Shows that the accrual component of earnings is less persistent than the cash component when forecasting next year.
formulas.trap: Extrapolating high-accrual earnings as a random walk; accruals reverse, so such earnings mean-revert faster.

formulas.name: Five-factor (extended) DuPont ROE
formulas.vars: Tax burden × interest burden × EBIT margin × asset turnover × financial leverage (average assets / average equity)
formulas.use: Decomposes ROE to show whether a change came from operations, taxes, the interest burden or leverage.
formulas.trap: Reading a higher interest burden ratio (EBT/EBIT) as more interest; a higher ratio means less interest and is favorable.

formulas.name: Core ROE excluding associates
formulas.use: Strips equity-method income and the investment out of ROE to measure the return on the company's own operations.
formulas.trap: Removing equity income from NI but leaving the investment in equity and assets, which understates core ROE and turnover.

formulas.name: FCFF from CFO by interest classification
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} FCFF = CFO + Int\,(1 - t) - FCInv \quad \text{(interest in CFO)} \\ FCFF = CFO - Int \times t - FCInv \quad \text{(interest in CFF)} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Int = interest paid; FCInv = fixed capital investment; the second line removes the interest tax shield still embedded in CFO
formulas.use: Builds FCFF from reported CFO after checking whether an IFRS reporter put interest paid in operating or financing.
formulas.trap: Adding after-tax interest back to an IFRS CFO that already excludes interest paid, which double-counts it.

formulas.name: LIFO-to-FIFO restatement
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} Inv_{FIFO} = Inv_{LIFO} + \text{LIFO reserve} \\ COGS_{FIFO} = COGS_{LIFO} - \Delta\text{LIFO reserve} \end{gathered}
formulas.use: Puts a US GAAP LIFO reporter on the FIFO basis of IFRS peers before comparing margins, turnover and leverage.
formulas.trap: Adding the full reserve to equity; equity rises by reserve × (1 − t) and the deferred tax liability by reserve × t.

definitions.term: Consolidation vs equity method ratio effects
definitions.def: Consolidation adds 100% of the investee's revenue, assets and liabilities (with NCI); the equity method shows one line. NI to the parent is the same, so net margin and ROA are lower when consolidated.

A joint venture gives rights to net assets and uses the equity method under IFRS 11 and US GAAP; a joint operation gives rights to specific assets and obligations, which each party recognizes directly.
An entity controlled through contracts rather than voting equity. Under US GAAP the primary beneficiary (power plus exposure to losses or benefits) consolidates it, even with 0% of the voting shares.
Debt: amortized cost (hold to collect + SPPI), FVOCI (collect and sell) or FVPL. Equity: FVPL unless FVOCI is irrevocably elected, and FVOCI equity gains are never recycled to profit or loss.
Equity-settled awards are fixed at grant-date fair value; cash-settled awards such as SARs are liabilities remeasured at fair value each period, so their expense swings with the share price.
A higher discount rate lowers the PBO (ΔPBO/PBO ≈ −D × Δr) and service cost; higher salary growth or longevity raises them. The interest-cost effect is ambiguous: higher rate, smaller PBO.
Only service cost is operating: adjusted EBIT = EBIT + P&L pension cost − service cost. Interest cost moves to interest expense and the actual return on assets to non-operating income.
LC functional (self-contained sub): current rate method, translation adjustment in OCI. Parent currency functional (integrated sub): temporal method, remeasurement gain or loss in net income.
ETR = Σ w_j × t_j, where w_j is each jurisdiction's share of pretax profit. A shift in profit mix toward low-tax countries lowers it; one-off settlements or allowance releases do not recur.
g_organic ≈ g_reported − g_FX − g_M&A. Growth from translating foreign sales at a weaker reporting currency is not operating growth and reverses when that currency strengthens.
Bank rating framework: Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management capability, Earnings sufficiency, Liquidity position and Sensitivity to market risk, each scored from 1 (best) to 5.

definitions.term: IFRS 9 ECL stages vs US GAAP CECL
definitions.def: ECL = PD × LGD × EAD. IFRS 9 books 12-month ECL in stage 1 and lifetime ECL once credit risk rises significantly (stages 2–3); US GAAP CECL books lifetime ECL on all loans from day one.
Reporting quality is whether reports faithfully represent results; earnings quality is whether those results are sustainable. Accurate reports can still show low-quality, non-recurring earnings.
Z = 1.2 WC/TA + 1.4 RE/TA + 3.3 EBIT/TA + 0.6 MVE/TL + 1.0 Sales/TA. A higher Z means lower bankruptcy risk, the opposite of the M-score; cutoffs suit manufacturers, not banks.
Moving items between categories without changing totals: recurring costs labeled non-recurring to lift core profit, or operating outflows capitalized so they sit in CFI instead of CFO.

definitions.term: IFRS vs US GAAP cash flow classification
definitions.def: US GAAP puts interest paid, interest received and dividends received in CFO and dividends paid in CFF. IFRS lets interest paid sit in CFO or CFF, so read the note before comparing CFO.

distractors: Equity income with excess purchase price amortization
Plan assets roll-forward and funded status
drill.why: A beginning balance plus the share of income less the share of dividends is the equity-method carrying value. Equity income alone stops at s × NI − Amort and never subtracts dividends received.

distractors: Equity income with excess purchase price amortization
drill.why: Whole-target fair value minus net assets versus price minus the parent's share of net assets is the full vs partial goodwill split. NCI multiplies a fair value by (1 − s) and subtracts nothing.

distractors: Plan assets roll-forward and funded status
Pension cost in P&L: IFRS vs US GAAP
drill.why: Service cost, interest at the discount rate on the opening balance and actuarial losses build the obligation, so this is the PBO roll-forward. Plan assets grow with the actual return and contributions instead.

drill.drillLatex: \begin{gathered} ? = PBO_{end} - PBO_{beg} + B - R_{actual} \\ ? = C - (FS_{end} - FS_{beg}) \end{gathered}
distractors: Plan assets roll-forward and funded status
CFO adjustment for contributions vs TPPC
drill.why: Contributions minus the change in funded status, or the PBO change plus benefits minus the actual return, is total periodic pension cost. The CFO adjustment starts from C − TPPC and applies (1 − t).

distractors: Translated ROA under the current rate method
drill.why: Net monetary position times the rate change is the temporal-method remeasurement gain or loss in net income. The current rate CTA uses net assets as the exposure and goes to OCI.
Common equity after deductions over risk-weighted assets is the CET1 ratio. The Tier 1 ratio adds AT1 to the numerator; the leverage ratio divides Tier 1 by unweighted exposure.
Tier 1 over unweighted total exposure with a 3% floor is the Basel III leverage ratio. The Tier 1 ratio uses the same numerator but divides by risk-weighted assets with a 6% minimum.
Weighted available stable funding over weighted required stable funding is the one-year NSFR. The LCR also has a 100% floor but divides HQLA by 30-day stressed net outflows.

distractors: Beneish DSRI, GMI and DEPI indices
drill.why: The change in NOA, or NI minus CFO and CFI, scaled by average NOA is the accruals ratio. The persistence regression splits earnings into cash and accruals but has no NOA scaling.

formulas.name: EPS after a debt- or cash-funded repurchase
formulas.latex: EPS_{new} = \frac{NI - D \times r_d\,(1 - t)}{n - D / P_{rep}}
formulas.vars: D = amount spent on the buyback; r_d = pre-tax rate on new debt, or the yield forgone on cash used; P_rep = repurchase price; n = shares before the buyback
formulas.use: Tests whether a borrowed buyback is accretive: EPS rises only if the after-tax cost of debt is below the earnings yield E/P.
formulas.trap: Comparing the pre-tax rate, or the cost of equity, with the earnings yield; the test is r_d(1 − t) versus E/P at P_rep.

formulas.name: BVPS after a share repurchase
formulas.vars: BV = book value of equity before the buyback; n_rep = shares repurchased; P_rep = repurchase price per share
formulas.use: Shows the book value per share effect of a repurchase: BVPS falls when P_rep > BVPS and rises when P_rep < BVPS.
formulas.trap: Assuming every buyback raises BVPS; paying above book value per share removes more equity per share and lowers BVPS.

formulas.name: Dividend and FCFE coverage ratios
formulas.use: Judges dividend safety; FCFE coverage near or below 1 means distributions rely on cash reserves or new borrowing.
formulas.trap: Relying on earnings coverage alone; accrual NI can cover the dividend while FCFE cannot fund dividends plus buybacks.

formulas.name: Target payout adjustment model
formulas.vars: p* = target payout ratio; EPS_1 = expected EPS; 1/N = adjustment factor, where N = years over which the gap is closed
formulas.use: Forecasts next year's dividend for a firm with a stable policy that moves gradually toward its target payout.
formulas.trap: Setting the dividend at p* × EPS immediately, or multiplying the gap by N instead of by the adjustment factor 1/N.

formulas.name: Residual dividend
formulas.vars: w_e = equity weight in the target capital structure; capital budget = total spending on positive-NPV projects
formulas.use: Sets the payout as the earnings left after funding the equity share of all positive-NPV projects at the target structure.
formulas.trap: Deducting the full capital budget from earnings instead of only its equity-financed share w_e.

formulas.name: WACC with target weights
formulas.latex: WACC = w_d\, r_d (1 - t) + w_p\, r_p + w_e\, r_e
formulas.vars: w = target market-value weights (pro forma weights after a restructuring); r_d = marginal pre-tax yield on new debt; t = marginal tax rate
formulas.use: Discount rate for FCFF and average-risk projects; recompute it with pro forma weights after an acquisition or recap.
formulas.trap: Using book-value weights or the coupon on old debt, or discounting FCFE at WACC instead of at the cost of equity.

formulas.name: After-tax cost of debt
formulas.vars: r_d = YTM on the firm's traded bonds, or the yield on bonds with the same (or synthetic) rating and maturity
formulas.use: Sets the marginal cost of new borrowing for WACC whether the firm has traded debt or only a credit rating.
formulas.trap: Using the historical coupon or the average tax rate; the cost of debt is today's marginal yield × (1 − marginal tax rate).

formulas.name: Forward-looking ERP (Gordon growth)
formulas.vars: D_1/P_0 = forward dividend yield on the market index; g = long-run dividend growth; r_LT,gov = long-term government bond yield
formulas.use: Estimates the market equity risk premium from the index dividend yield plus expected growth minus the long-term bond yield.
formulas.trap: Subtracting a T-bill yield; the forward-looking GGM premium is measured against the long-term government bond yield.

formulas.name: Macroeconomic ERP (Ibbotson–Chen)
formulas.latex: ERP = \left[(1 + i)(1 + g_{rEPS})(1 + g_{PE}) - 1\right] + Y - r_f
formulas.vars: i = expected inflation; g_rEPS = real EPS growth; g_PE = growth in the P/E ratio; Y = expected income (dividend) yield; r_f = expected risk-free return
formulas.use: Builds the ERP from supply-side drivers when the estimate should be tied to expected economic growth.
formulas.trap: Adding inflation and growth instead of compounding them, or putting the income yield inside the compounded bracket.

formulas.name: Blume-adjusted beta
formulas.vars: beta_raw = regression beta against the market index over the estimation window (typically 2–5 years)
formulas.use: Shrinks a regression beta toward 1, because betas mean-revert, before using it in CAPM.
formulas.trap: Shrinking toward 0 or the industry mean, or putting the 2/3 weight on 1.0 instead of on the raw beta.

formulas.name: Unlevering and relevering beta
formulas.vars: beta_A = asset (unlevered) beta; D/E = comparable's market D/E; relever at the subject's target D/E and tax rate; debt beta assumed zero
formulas.use: Pure-play method: converts a comparable's equity beta into a project or private-firm equity beta at its own leverage.
formulas.trap: Relevering at the comparable's D/E or tax rate instead of the subject's, or using D/(D + E) where the formula needs D/E.

formulas.name: Country risk premium (sovereign spread method)
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} CRP = (y_{sov} - y_{dev}) \times \frac{\sigma_{equity}}{\sigma_{sov\ bond}} \\ r_e = r_f + \beta\,(ERP + CRP) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: y_sov = EM sovereign yield on USD debt; y_dev = developed benchmark yield, same maturity; sigma = volatility of the EM equity and sovereign bond markets
formulas.use: Scales the sovereign default spread up to equity risk and adds it to the developed-market ERP for an emerging-market firm.
formulas.trap: Adding the raw sovereign spread without the volatility ratio, or inverting the ratio so the premium shrinks below the spread.

formulas.name: Build-up cost of equity
formulas.latex: r_e = r_f + ERP + SP + IP + SCRP
formulas.vars: SP = size premium; IP = industry premium (if used); SCRP = company-specific risk premium; beta is implicitly 1
formulas.use: Estimates the cost of equity for a private or thinly traded firm that has no reliable beta.
formulas.trap: Multiplying ERP by a beta; build-up assumes beta = 1 and stacks premiums, while expanded CAPM uses a peer beta times ERP.

formulas.name: Bond-yield-plus-risk-premium cost of equity
formulas.vars: YTM = yield on the company's own long-term debt; RP = judgmental equity-over-debt premium, typically about 3–5 percentage points
formulas.use: Quick cost-of-equity cross-check for a public company that has traded long-term debt.
formulas.trap: Starting from the government bond yield; this method adds the premium to the company's own long-term debt yield.

formulas.name: Multifactor (Fama–French) cost of equity
formulas.vars: SMB = small-minus-big size premium; HML = high-minus-low value premium; the Pastor–Stambaugh model adds a liquidity factor
formulas.use: Estimates required return from exposures to market, size and value factors when one CAPM factor misprices the stock.
formulas.trap: Adding the full SMB or HML premium without its factor beta, which can be negative for large-cap or growth stocks.

formulas.name: Project-specific WACC
formulas.vars: beta_proj = pure-play equity beta relevered at the project's target D/E; weights = the project's target financing mix
formulas.use: Discount rate for a project whose risk differs from the firm's average, built from a pure-play beta.
formulas.trap: Using the parent's WACC because the parent funds the project; the rate depends on project risk, not the funding source.

formulas.name: MM Proposition I with taxes and static trade-off
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} V_L = V_U + tD \\ V_L = V_U + tD - PV(\text{distress costs}) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: tD = PV of the debt tax shield for permanent debt; distress costs = bankruptcy, agency and lost-business costs
formulas.use: Values leverage: the debt tax shield adds tD, and expected distress costs push the optimal debt level below 100%.
formulas.trap: Concluding the minimum-WACC structure is all debt; with distress costs WACC is U-shaped and the optimum is interior.

formulas.name: MM Proposition II with taxes
formulas.vars: r_0 = cost of capital of the all-equity firm; without taxes the (1 − t) term drops out and WACC stays constant
formulas.use: Shows how the cost of equity rises with leverage; with taxes it rises more slowly, so WACC falls as D/E increases.
formulas.trap: Dropping the (1 − t) factor in the with-tax version, or claiming WACC is constant with taxes, which is the no-tax result.

formulas.name: Pro forma EPS: stock vs cash deal
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} EPS_{stock} = \frac{NI_A + NI_T + S(1 - t)}{n_A + n_{new}} \\ EPS_{cash} = \frac{NI_A + NI_T + S(1 - t) - Cash \times r(1 - t)}{n_A} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: S = pre-tax synergies; n_new = shares issued to target holders; r = rate on new debt or interest forgone on cash used
formulas.use: Tests accretion or dilution; an all-stock deal without synergies is accretive when the acquirer's P/E exceeds the P/E paid.
formulas.trap: Treating EPS accretion as value creation; a high-P/E acquirer can report accretion while overpaying and destroying value.

formulas.name: Takeover premium
formulas.vars: DP = deal price per share; SP = target's unaffected (pre-announcement) share price
formulas.use: Measures the control premium in past deals and adds it to a comparable-company value to estimate a takeover price.
formulas.trap: Adding a takeover premium to a comparable-transaction value, which already includes control, so it is counted twice.

formulas.name: Merger gains to target and acquirer
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} Gain_T = P_T - V_T \\ Gain_A = S - (P_T - V_T) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: P_T = price paid for the target; V_T = target's pre-announcement market value; S = PV of synergies net of integration costs
formulas.use: Splits deal value: target holders receive the premium, and the acquirer keeps synergies minus the premium paid.
formulas.trap: Thinking the target's gain in a cash deal depends on synergies; it is fixed at the premium and the acquirer bears the risk.

formulas.name: Post-merger value of the combined firm
formulas.vars: V_A, V_T = pre-merger values; S = synergies; C = cash paid to target shareholders (zero in an all-stock deal)
formulas.use: Values the combined company after a deal; in a stock deal target holders own part of V_AT instead of receiving C.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to subtract the cash paid out, which overstates the combined firm's value to the acquirer's shareholders.

definitions.def: MM: in perfect markets investors make homemade dividends, so payout does not change value. Bird-in-hand: near-term dividends look less risky, lowering r_e; MM call this a fallacy.
Managers raise dividends only when confident future cash flow can sustain them, so an increase signals higher sustainable earnings and a cut signals lasting weakness; markets punish cuts hard.

Investor groups prefer different payouts (high-tax investors low, income-needing investors high), so firms attract matching clienteles. It explains who owns the stock, not which payout maximizes value.
The firm sets a price range and quantity; holders tender at their minimum price, and the firm accepts bids from the lowest upward and pays every accepted seller the single clearing price.
ESG factors are material when they are likely to affect revenue, costs, assets, liabilities or the cost of capital; they differ by industry, as SASB/ISSB industry standards map them.
Model quantifiable ESG effects in cash flows (carbon costs, capex, stranded-asset write-downs, terminal value) before adding a discount-rate premium, so the same risk is not counted twice.
With concentrated ownership (families, state, pyramids, dual-class shares) the main conflict is controlling vs minority holders, such as tunneling via related-party deals, not managers vs owners.
Average excess return of equities over government debt. Arithmetic means suit single-period CAPM, geometric means long horizons; estimates suffer survivorship bias and depend on the window.
Because managers know more than investors, firms use internal funds first, then debt, and new equity last; an equity issue signals overvaluation, so prices tend to fall on the announcement.
A spin-off distributes subsidiary shares pro rata to existing holders and raises no cash; an equity carve-out sells a minority stake in an IPO, raising cash while the parent keeps control.
Comparable company multiples give a non-control value, so a takeover premium is added. Comparable transaction multiples already include the control premium, so no premium is added.
Chapter 11 reorganizes the debtor as a going concern, often converting unsecured debt into new equity and wiping out old holders; Chapter 7 liquidates assets and pays claims by absolute priority.
Issuing debt to fund a large buyback or special dividend. It adds value through tax shields and cash-flow discipline when leverage was below target and cash flows are stable; it can also deter bids.
Divest when after-tax sale proceeds exceed the unit's value to the parent, meaning the PV of its cash flows inside the group including lost synergies, not its book value or a standalone multiple.

distractors: Pro forma EPS: stock vs cash deal
drill.why: Net income cut by after-tax interest on new debt over fewer shares (D / P_rep retired) is EPS after a debt-financed buyback. Pro forma deal EPS adds target income and synergies instead.
Closing a fraction 1/N of the gap between target payout × EPS and the last dividend is the target payout adjustment model. The residual model subtracts the equity-funded capital budget from NI.
Dividing by 1 + (1 − t)D/E strips financial leverage and multiplying by it relevers, so this is the pure-play beta. MM II also uses (1 − t)D/E but adds a spread to r_0, not a beta.
A sovereign spread scaled by equity-to-bond volatility is the country risk premium, added to the ERP inside CAPM. Bond-yield-plus adds a premium to the firm's own debt yield, not a scaled spread.
Stacking size, industry and company-specific premiums on r_f + ERP with no beta is the build-up method for private firms. Fama–French multiplies factor premiums by estimated betas.

distractors: MM Proposition I with taxes and static trade-off
drill.why: The cost of equity rising linearly in D/E, damped by (1 − t), is MM Proposition II with taxes. Proposition I with taxes values the firm (V_U + tD); it does not give a required return.

distractors: Post-merger value of the combined firm
Pro forma EPS: stock vs cash deal
drill.why: Target holders gain the premium P_T − V_T and the acquirer gains synergies minus that premium. The takeover premium ratio divides the price gap by the unaffected price, giving a percentage.

formulas.name: Perceived mispricing decomposition
formulas.vars: V_E = analyst's value estimate; P = market price; V = true intrinsic value; V_E - V = valuation error
formulas.use: Splits an estimate-versus-price gap into true mispricing and the analyst's own model error before calling a stock cheap.
formulas.trap: Treating the whole V_E - P gap as alpha; in a heavily followed stock most of the gap is more likely valuation error.

formulas.name: Growth rate implied by market price
formulas.use: Reverse-engineers the growth priced in to compare with b x ROE; rearranged, r = D_1/P_0 + g gives the implied return.
formulas.trap: Using D_0 instead of D_1, or forgetting that implied g rises one-for-one with the assumed required return r.

formulas.name: Gordon growth model and sensitivity to g
formulas.vars: Requires r > g; g may be negative for a shrinking dividend (r - g then exceeds r); the derivative holds D_1 fixed
formulas.use: Values a mature payer growing at a stable rate no higher than nominal GDP; the second line shows why g near r swings value.
formulas.trap: Dividing D_0 rather than D_1 by r - g, or computing r - g as 0.10 - 0.04 when g = -4% (correct: 0.14).

formulas.name: No-growth value plus PVGO
formulas.use: Splits price into current earnings as a no-growth perpetuity plus growth opportunities; the P/E line shows the growth share.
formulas.trap: Using trailing E_0 in E_1/r, or assuming retention creates PVGO; reinvesting at ROE below r makes PVGO negative.

formulas.name: Two-stage DDM
formulas.use: Values a stock with an explicit high-growth period of n years followed by stable growth g_L forever.
formulas.trap: Computing P_n with D_n instead of D_{n+1}, or discounting P_n over n + 1 periods; P_n sits at time n.

formulas.name: H-model
formulas.vars: H = half the number of years over which growth declines linearly from g_S to g_L
formulas.use: Approximates value when growth fades linearly from a high short-term rate to a long-run rate instead of dropping at once.
formulas.trap: Using the full fade period as H instead of half, or using D_1 in the second term; the extra-growth term uses D_0.

formulas.name: Three-stage DDM with H-model end stage
formulas.vars: V_n^H = H-model value at time n with D_n as the base dividend; alternative build: explicit stages 1-2, Gordon at the end of stage 2
formulas.use: Values growth, transition and mature phases: discount stage-1 dividends one by one, then an H-model value for stages 2-3.
formulas.trap: Discounting V_n^H over n + 1 periods, or using D_0 instead of D_n as the H-model base dividend at time n.

formulas.name: Sustainable growth rate (PRAT)
formulas.vars: b = retention ratio = 1 - payout = (NI - D)/NI; ROE on beginning equity; PRAT = profit margin, retention, asset turnover, leverage
formulas.use: Growth financed by retained earnings at constant leverage; feeds g in Gordon, justified multiples and terminal stages.
formulas.trap: Multiplying ROE by the payout ratio instead of the retention ratio, or using a temporarily high ROE for terminal growth.

formulas.name: FCFF from net income
formulas.latex: FCFF = NI + NCC + Int(1-t) - FCInv - WCInv
formulas.vars: NCC = net noncash charges (D&A, impairments; subtract noncash gains); FCInv = capex - asset-sale proceeds
formulas.use: Cash flow to all capital providers built from the income statement; discount at WACC to get firm value.
formulas.trap: Adding back pre-tax interest, or leaving a noncash gain on sale in NI while also netting the sale proceeds in FCInv.

formulas.name: FCFF from EBIT and EBITDA
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} FCFF = EBIT(1-t) + Dep - FCInv - WCInv \\ FCFF = EBITDA(1-t) + Dep \cdot t - FCInv - WCInv \end{gathered}
formulas.use: FCFF from operating profit; from EBITDA add back only the depreciation tax shield, since depreciation was never deducted.
formulas.trap: Adding back full depreciation when starting from EBITDA, or subtracting after-tax interest from EBIT.

formulas.name: FCFF and FCFE from CFO
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} FCFF = CFO + Int(1-t) - FCInv \\ FCFE = CFO - FCInv + \text{Net borrowing} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: CFO already nets working-capital investment and (US GAAP) interest paid; under IFRS, interest classified in CFF is not added back
formulas.use: Quickest route from the cash flow statement, because CFO already includes noncash charges and working-capital changes.
formulas.trap: Subtracting WCInv again from CFO, or adding back interest that an IFRS filer already classified in financing cash flow.

formulas.name: FCFE from FCFF or net income
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} FCFE = FCFF - Int(1-t) + \text{Net borrowing} \\ FCFE = NI + NCC - FCInv - WCInv + \text{Net borrowing} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Net borrowing = new debt issued - debt repaid; dividends, buybacks and share issues are uses of FCFE, not inputs
formulas.use: Cash available to common shareholders after all debt flows; discount at r_e for equity value directly.
formulas.trap: Capitalizing a debt-funded spike in FCFE in terminal value, or subtracting dividends or buybacks to reach FCFE.

formulas.name: FCFE forecast with a target debt ratio
formulas.vars: DR = target share of net new investment financed with debt; often applied per share (EPS, capex and Dep per share)
formulas.use: Forecasts FCFE when a fixed share of net investment is debt-funded, avoiding separate debt issue and repayment forecasts.
formulas.trap: Applying (1 - DR) to gross capex instead of capex net of depreciation, or forgetting to apply it to WCInv.

formulas.name: Working capital investment
formulas.use: Increase in operating working capital, which reduces FCFF and FCFE in the year it occurs.
formulas.trap: Including the change in cash or in notes payable and current debt; cash is excluded and short-term debt is net borrowing.

formulas.name: FCFE valuation, general and single-stage
formulas.use: Equity value from FCFE at r_e; use when dividends differ from capacity or for a control view. Firm analog: FCFF_1/(WACC - g).
formulas.trap: Subtracting debt from an FCFE-based value, or putting FCFE_0 rather than FCFE_1 over r_e - g.

formulas.name: Two-stage FCFE model
formulas.use: Values equity with high FCFE growth for n years, then stable growth; the per-share result needs no debt deduction.
formulas.trap: Carrying high-growth reinvestment into FCFE_{n+1}; stable-stage FCFE should reflect lower net investment needs.

formulas.name: FCFF terminal value and its present value
formulas.use: Terminal value at the end of an explicit FCFF forecast; add its PV to the PV of explicit FCFF to get firm value.
formulas.trap: Dividing FCFF_N rather than FCFF_{N+1} by WACC - g, or discounting TV_N over N + 1 periods.

formulas.name: Equity value per share from firm value
formulas.vars: V_ops = PV of operating FCFF; NOA = market value of non-operating assets (excess cash, non-core investments); D, P = market values of debt, preferred
formulas.use: Converts operating firm value from an FCFF model into value per share for comparison with the market price.
formulas.trap: Forgetting preferred or NCI, adding excess cash whose interest is already in FCFF, or dividing by basic shares.

formulas.name: Justified leading P/E
formulas.vars: 1 - b = payout ratio; multiplied by E_{n+1} it also sets the terminal price P_n in a multistage DDM
formulas.use: P/E warranted by payout, r and g from the Gordon model; an actual P/E above it signals overvaluation.
formulas.trap: Raising payout while holding g fixed; g = b x ROE falls as payout rises, so the net effect depends on ROE versus r.

formulas.name: Justified trailing P/E
formulas.use: Justified multiple on trailing EPS; it exceeds the justified leading P/E by the factor (1 + g).
formulas.trap: Applying a trailing multiple to forward EPS, or a leading multiple to trailing EPS, which mis-counts one year of growth.

formulas.name: Justified price-to-book ratio
formulas.use: P/B warranted by fundamentals; it exceeds 1 only when ROE exceeds r. Suits banks and asset-heavy firms.
formulas.trap: Calling P/B below 1 cheap without checking ROE; a bank earning ROE below r deserves a P/B under 1.

formulas.name: Justified price-to-sales ratio
formulas.vars: E_0/S_0 = net profit margin; equals the justified trailing P/E times the margin
formulas.use: P/S warranted by net margin, payout, r and g; useful when earnings are negative or volatile but sales are positive.
formulas.trap: Comparing P/S across peers with different margins or leverage; P/S puts an equity price over firm-level sales.

formulas.name: Normalized EPS, average ROE method
formulas.vars: ROE bar = average ROE over a full business cycle; the historical average EPS method uses mean EPS over the cycle instead
formulas.use: Normalizes a cyclical firm's EPS before applying P/E; reflects current size, unlike the historical average EPS method.
formulas.trap: Using trough-year EPS (P/E looks high) or historical average EPS for a firm that has grown over the cycle.

formulas.name: Earnings yield
formulas.use: Ranks stocks when some EPS are negative or near zero; E/P stays continuous through zero, and higher means cheaper.
formulas.trap: Treating a negative P/E as cheap or dropping loss-makers; ranked on E/P, loss-makers simply fall to the bottom.

formulas.name: PEG ratio
formulas.vars: g = expected EPS growth in decimal, so g x 100 is growth in percentage points
formulas.use: Growth-adjusted P/E; a lower PEG looks cheaper per point of growth among peers with similar risk.
formulas.trap: Dividing by g in decimals (20/0.15 = 133), or ignoring that PEG disregards risk and how long growth lasts.

formulas.name: Harmonic mean of multiples
formulas.use: Averages peer multiples through their inverses; the weighted form equals a value-weighted portfolio or index P/E.
