formulas.trap: Assuming it removes all outlier bias; it damps large multiples but is pulled toward unusually small ones.

formulas.name: Enterprise value and EV multiples
formulas.vars: Cash includes short-term investments; EV and EBITDA (or sales) are both pre-financing, so leverage does not distort the ratio
formulas.use: Compares firms with different leverage or heavy D&A; EV/sales replaces P/S for loss-making or highly levered firms.
formulas.trap: Putting market cap over EBITDA or sales, or comparing EV/EBITDA across firms with very different capex needs.

formulas.name: Standardized unexpected earnings (SUE)
formulas.use: Momentum indicator that scales an earnings surprise by past forecast-error volatility so surprises compare across firms.
formulas.trap: Ranking on raw dollar surprise, or treating SUE as a fundamentals-based value estimate rather than a momentum signal.

formulas.name: Justified P/E with inflation pass-through
formulas.vars: rho = real required return; I = inflation; lambda = share of inflation passed through to earnings (1 = full); assumes zero real growth
formulas.use: Explains why a lower P/E in a high-inflation country can be fair when firms cannot pass inflation into earnings.
formulas.trap: Assuming inflation always lowers P/E; with full pass-through (lambda = 1) P/E = 1/rho whatever the inflation rate.

formulas.name: Yardeni model justified market P/E
formulas.vars: CBY = Moody's A-rated corporate bond yield; LTEG = consensus five-year earnings growth; b = weight on growth, historically about 0.10
formulas.use: Justified market P/E from corporate bond yields and expected growth; an actual P/E above it suggests an overvalued market.
formulas.trap: Using the Treasury yield (that is the Fed model) or adding b x LTEG to the bond yield instead of subtracting it.

formulas.name: Residual income
formulas.use: Earnings above the required return on beginning book equity; per share, roll book forward each year with clean surplus.
formulas.trap: Charging r_e on ending book or market cap, or keeping the charge at r_e x B_0 instead of updating book each year.

formulas.name: Residual income valuation model
formulas.use: Intrinsic value as current book plus PV of expected RI; recognizes value earlier, so terminal value matters less.
formulas.trap: Adding the PV of NI rather than RI to book value, which double-counts the required return on existing equity.

formulas.name: Clean surplus relation
formulas.use: Rolls book value forward for RI forecasts; RI is valid only if all equity changes except owner transactions pass NI.
formulas.trap: Ignoring OCI items (FX translation, pension remeasurement) that bypass NI and leave forecast RI misstated.

formulas.name: Single-stage residual income model
formulas.use: Value with constant ROE, r and g; dividing by B_0 gives justified P/B. Solve for g to find the growth implied by price.
formulas.trap: Putting ROE - g in the RI term (that is the P/B form), or assuming ROE stays above r forever without fading.

formulas.name: Finite-horizon RI with persistence factor
formulas.vars: omega = persistence factor from 0 to 1: 1 = RI continues at RI_T forever, 0 = RI ends after year T
formulas.use: Fades residual income after the explicit horizon; use a low omega for extreme ROE, special items or large accruals.
formulas.trap: Discounting the continuing term by (1 + r)^T instead of (1 + r)^(T-1), or thinking omega = 0 drops RI_T itself.

formulas.name: Multistage RI with terminal premium over book
formulas.vars: P_T - B_T = forecast premium of price over book at T (e.g., from a terminal P/B), equal to the value at T of all RI after T
formulas.use: Values a stock when a horizon P/B can be forecast; the premium over book at T captures all continuing residual income.
formulas.trap: Adding the full terminal price P_T instead of only the premium over book, which counts book value B_T twice.

formulas.name: Economic value added and market value added
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} EVA = NOPAT - WACC \times TC \\ MVA = V_{firm} - TC \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: TC = total capital invested (debt + equity); NOPAT = EBIT(1 - t) after adjustments such as capitalized R&D
formulas.use: Firm-level value creation: EVA charges WACC on all capital; MVA is the market's capitalization of expected future EVA.
formulas.trap: Using NI instead of NOPAT in EVA, or charging WACC on book equity only, which mixes firm and equity levels.

formulas.name: Capitalized cash flow method
formulas.use: Single-stage value of a stable private firm: FCFF at WACC for firm value or FCFE at r_e for equity value.
formulas.trap: Capitalizing current FCF_0 instead of next year's normalized FCF_1, or capitalizing FCFF at the equity rate.

formulas.name: Excess earnings method: intangibles value
formulas.vars: EE = normalized earnings - required returns on working capital and fixed assets; firm value = WC + fixed assets + V_int
formulas.use: Values a small firm's intangibles by capitalizing earnings above the required returns on its tangible assets.
formulas.trap: Capitalizing total normalized earnings at the intangible rate, or forgetting to add working capital and fixed assets.

formulas.name: Expanded CAPM required return (private firm)
formulas.vars: beta = guideline public company beta; SP = size premium; SCR = company-specific risk premium; the beta-free build-up method is under Corporate issuers
formulas.use: Required return on equity for a private firm when a guideline-company beta is available, plus size and specific-risk premiums.
formulas.trap: Adding an illiquidity premium to the rate and then also applying a DLOM, which penalizes the same illiquidity twice.

formulas.name: Discount for lack of control from control premium
formulas.use: Converts an observed control premium into the discount from a controlling value down to a minority value.
formulas.trap: Setting DLOC equal to the control premium; a 30% premium implies a 23.1% DLOC, not 30%.

formulas.name: Total discount for lack of control and marketability
formulas.use: Combines DLOC and DLOM multiplicatively to move from a controlling, marketable value to a minority, nonmarketable one.
formulas.trap: Adding the discounts (23.1% + 20% = 43.1%) instead of compounding them (38.5%), or applying DLOC to a minority value.

definitions.def: Going-concern value assumes the firm keeps operating; liquidation value is the breakup value of assets net of liabilities, orderly or forced. Use liquidation value when it exceeds going-concern value.

definitions.term: Investment value vs fair market value
definitions.def: Investment value is the worth to a specific buyer, including its synergies and financing; fair market value is the price between hypothetical willing, informed parties at arm's length and excludes buyer synergies.
Market value below the sum-of-the-parts value of segments net of debt and head-office costs. Proposed causes: internal capital inefficiency, endogenous factors and research measurement error.
DDM fits dividend payers whose payout is tied to profitability, valued from a minority view. It matches FCFE value only if dividends equal FCFE; a control buyer values FCFE or FCFF instead.
Use FCFF at WACC for highly levered firms, negative FCFE or a changing capital structure, then subtract debt; use FCFE at r_e when leverage is stable and debt flows are predictable.
Excess cash and non-core investments are kept out of forecast FCFF and added at market value; keeping their income in FCFF and also adding the asset counts the same value twice.

Comparables value a stock relative to peer multiples (law of one price) and give only relative value; forecasted fundamentals derive a justified multiple from r, g and payout, anchoring intrinsic value.

Compares the S&P 500 earnings yield (E/P) with the 10-year Treasury yield; an E/P below the yield signals overvalued stocks. It ignores growth and the equity risk premium and compares a real yield with a nominal one.
P/CF uses cash flow per share defined as EPS plus noncash charges, CFO, FCFE or EBITDA. Cash flow is harder to manipulate than EPS, but EPS plus noncash charges ignores working-capital changes.

Market value of debt and equity divided by the replacement cost of total assets. Unlike P/B it uses replacement cost and firm-level value; q above 1 means the market values the assets above their cost.

After the horizon, RI may persist (omega = 1), drop to zero (omega = 0), fade (0 < omega < 1) or fade as ROE reverts to the industry mean. Persistence is lower with extreme ROE, special items and big accruals.

Guideline public company multiples come from minority, marketable trading prices; guideline transaction multiples come from whole-company deals, so they embed a control premium and possibly synergies.

Estimated from restricted stock studies, pre-IPO transaction studies or the price of an at-the-money put with term equal to the holding period. Larger with no exit route, high volatility or no dividends.

distractors: FCFE from FCFF or net income
drill.why: Adding back after-tax interest to net income gives the flow to debt and equity holders, so this is FCFF. FCFE from net income drops the interest add-back and adds net borrowing instead.

distractors: FCFE from FCFF or net income
drill.why: Only the equity-funded share (1 - DR) of net investment is subtracted, which is the target-debt-ratio FCFE forecast. FCFE from net income subtracts all of FCInv and WCInv and adds net borrowing explicitly.

distractors: Gordon growth model and sensitivity to g
Three-stage DDM with H-model end stage
drill.why: A Gordon value at g_L plus a premium D_0 x H x (g_S - g_L) for linearly fading growth is the H-model. The two-stage DDM discounts explicit dividends and a terminal price, with growth dropping abruptly.

Payout times (1 + g) over r - g prices trailing earnings E_0, so this is the trailing P/E. The leading P/E omits (1 + g) because E_1 already includes a year of growth; P/S also multiplies by the net margin.
ROE - g over r - g is price over book and equals 1 when ROE = r. The single-stage RI model expresses the same economics in dollars, B_0 plus (ROE - r)B_0/(r - g), not as a ratio.

Book value plus constant-growth residual income (ROE - r)B_0 capitalized at r - g is the single-stage RI model. The persistence model fades RI at omega after an explicit horizon instead of growing it at g.
The (1 + r - omega) term marks RI decaying at persistence omega after year T, so this is the finite-horizon RI model. The single-stage RI model grows RI at g forever from today, with no omega.

distractors: Total discount for lack of control and marketability
drill.why: One minus the inverse of (1 + control premium) turns a premium measured up from minority value into a discount measured down from control value: DLOC. The total discount compounds DLOC with DLOM instead.

distractors: Gordon growth model and sensitivity to g
drill.why: E_1/r capitalizes current earnings with no growth, so the rest of the price is the present value of growth opportunities. The Gordon model instead divides D_1 by r - g, building growth into the denominator.
The justified trailing P/E multiplied by the net margin E_0/S_0 turns earnings into sales, so this is the justified P/S. The trailing P/E has the same payout x (1 + g) over r - g but no margin term.

Next-period FCFF over WACC - g, set at horizon N, is the FCFF terminal value, discounted N periods. The capitalized cash flow method uses the same structure at time 0 to value a stable private firm outright.

distractors: Economic value added and market value added
drill.why: Net income minus an equity charge on beginning book value is residual income, an equity-level measure. EVA instead subtracts a WACC charge on total capital from NOPAT, a firm-level measure.

formulas.name: Arbitrage-free bond value from spot rates
formulas.vars: z_t = benchmark spot (zero) rate for year t; DF_t = 1/(1+z_t)^t = discount factor
formulas.use: Prices an option-free bond by discounting each cash flow at its own spot rate; the YTM is the single rate giving the same price.
formulas.trap: Discounting every cash flow at one YTM and calling it arbitrage-free; YTM is a blend of spot rates and differs by coupon level.

formulas.name: Bootstrapping spot rates from par rates
formulas.vars: c_n = coupon per 100 of the n-year par bond; z_1 to z_{n-1} are already solved, so z_n is the only unknown
formulas.use: Extracts the n-year spot rate from the n-year par rate once all shorter spot rates are known, one maturity at a time.
formulas.trap: Discounting the early coupons at the par rate; each coupon uses its own earlier spot rate and only the final cash flow uses z_n.

formulas.name: Par rate (swap rate) from discount factors
formulas.vars: s_n = n-period par rate per period; on the swap (SOFR) curve this is the n-year swap rate
formulas.use: Gives the coupon that prices a bond at par on a given spot curve, which is also the fixed rate of an n-period swap.
formulas.trap: Putting only the final discount factor in the denominator; the annuity term is the sum of all discount factors through n.

formulas.name: Implied forward rate from spot rates
formulas.vars: f_{A,B-A} = rate for B - A years starting in year A (2y3y: A = 2, B = 5); f_{0,1} = z_1; the spot rate is the geometric mean of 1-year forwards
formulas.use: Gives the break-even rate locked in between two future dates, such as 1y1y or 2y3y, from today's spot curve.
formulas.trap: Skipping the 1/(B - A) root, or reading 2y3y as a 2-year loan; it is a 3-year rate that starts in 2 years.

formulas.name: Forward pricing model
formulas.vars: F_{A,B-A} = forward price at time A, per 1 of face, of a zero-coupon bond maturing at B; DF = spot discount factors
formulas.use: Prices a forward contract on a zero: buying the B-year zero today equals buying the A-year zero plus the forward.
formulas.trap: Inverting the ratio; the forward price is below 1 and equals the longer discount factor divided by the shorter one.

formulas.name: Rolling down the yield curve return
formulas.vars: P_1^roll = price one period later at today's yield for the shorter remaining maturity (curve unchanged); C = coupon received
formulas.use: Estimates the one-period return from holding a bond as it ages down a stable upward-sloping curve: coupon plus rolldown.
formulas.trap: Pricing P_1 at the original maturity's yield, which captures only accretion; roll-down gain needs the shorter maturity's lower yield.

formulas.name: Swap spread and I-spread
formulas.vars: s_T = T-year swap (SOFR) rate; y_T^Treasury = on-the-run government yield of the same tenor; y_bond = the bond's YTM
formulas.use: Swap spread prices swap-curve credit and liquidity over governments; the I-spread prices a bond's yield over the swap curve.
formulas.trap: Swapping the benchmarks: the swap spread is measured over the government yield, the I-spread over the swap rate.

formulas.name: Key rate duration price change
formulas.vars: KRD_k = sensitivity to a shift in key par rate k alone; Delta r_k = change in that key rate (decimal)
formulas.use: Estimates price change from non-parallel curve moves (steepening, twists, curvature) by summing exposures to each key rate.
formulas.trap: Using effective duration for a non-parallel shift; two portfolios with equal duration can have different KRDs and losses.

formulas.name: Equilibrium models: CIR and Vasicek
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{CIR: } dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dz \\ \text{Vasicek: } dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\,dz \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: k = speed of mean reversion; theta = long-run short rate; sigma = volatility; dz = random shock
formulas.use: Models short-rate dynamics with mean reversion; CIR volatility rises with the rate level, Vasicek volatility is constant.
formulas.trap: Thinking Vasicek rates stay positive; only CIR's square-root term keeps rates non-negative, and neither model fits today's curve exactly.

formulas.name: Adjacent rates in a lognormal binomial tree
formulas.vars: r_U, r_L = adjacent higher and lower one-period forward rates at the same date; sigma = annual rate volatility; t = years per period
formulas.use: Spaces adjacent nodes at each date of a lognormal rate tree; the lowest rate is then solved by calibrating to par bonds.
formulas.trap: Using e^{sigma} instead of e^{2 sigma}; adjacent nodes sit two volatility steps apart, and the lognormal form keeps rates positive.

formulas.name: Option-free bond value at a tree node
formulas.vars: V_U, V_L = bond values at the up and down nodes one period later; C = coupon paid then; r_node = one-period rate at this node
formulas.use: Backward induction: averages the next-period values plus coupon and discounts at this node's one-period forward rate.
formulas.trap: Discounting at a time-0 spot rate instead of the node's own one-period rate, or dropping the coupon from the up and down values.

formulas.name: Pathwise and Monte Carlo valuation
formulas.vars: PV_j = bond value discounted along rate path j; N = number of paths; sigma_PV = standard deviation of path values
formulas.use: Values a bond as the average PV across rate paths; Monte Carlo samples paths for path-dependent cash flows such as MBS.
formulas.trap: Expecting more paths to fix model error; SE falls only with root N, and a drift adjustment is still needed to match benchmarks.

formulas.name: Arbitrage-free models: Ho-Lee and KWF
formulas.vars: theta_t = time-varying drift calibrated to today's benchmark prices; sigma = volatility; KWF = Kalotay-Williams-Fabozzi
formulas.use: Short-rate models whose time-dependent drift is calibrated so they reprice today's benchmark bonds exactly.
formulas.trap: Ho-Lee rates are normal and can turn negative; KWF models ln r, so rates are lognormal. Neither model is mean-reverting.

formulas.name: Callable and putable bond values
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} V_{\text{callable}} = V_{\text{straight}} - V_{\text{call}} \\ V_{\text{putable}} = V_{\text{straight}} + V_{\text{put}} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: V_straight = value of the identical option-free bond; the issuer owns the call, the investor owns the put
formulas.use: Splits a bond with an embedded option into a straight bond and the option, then values the option as the difference.
formulas.trap: Mixing signs: higher volatility raises both option values, so it lowers the callable's value but raises the putable's value.

formulas.name: Callable and putable node values
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} V_{\text{call node}} = \min\left(\text{call price},\ V_{\text{hold}}\right) \\ V_{\text{put node}} = \max\left(\text{put price},\ V_{\text{hold}}\right) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: V_hold = [0.5(V_U + C) + 0.5(V_L + C)] / (1 + r_node), the discounted continuation value, excluding the coupon paid at this node
formulas.use: Applies the exercise rule at every node on or after the first exercise date while backward-inducting through the tree.
formulas.trap: Applying min/max before the option is exercisable, or comparing the call price with a value that includes this node's coupon.

formulas.name: Z-spread
formulas.vars: z_t = benchmark spot rates; Z = constant spread added to every spot rate; CF_t = promised cash flows
formulas.use: Finds the constant spread over every benchmark spot rate that equates promised cash flows with the market price.
formulas.trap: Using the Z-spread on a bond with options; it ignores how cash flows change with rates, so it still contains the option cost.

formulas.name: Option-adjusted spread and option cost
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} P_{\text{mkt}} = V_{\text{tree}}\left(r_{\text{node}} + OAS\right) \\ \text{Option cost} = Z\text{-spread} - OAS \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: OAS = constant spread added to every one-period rate in the tree; option cost is positive for callables, negative for putables
formulas.use: OAS is the spread that reprices the bond on the tree after removing the option; compare OAS, not Z-spread, across callables.
formulas.trap: Higher assumed volatility makes the call worth more, so a callable's computed OAS falls (a putable's OAS rises).

formulas.name: Effective duration
formulas.vars: PV_-, PV_+ = values after the benchmark curve shifts down and up by Delta Curve (decimal), holding OAS constant
formulas.use: Measures price sensitivity to a parallel benchmark curve shift for bonds whose cash flows change with rates.
formulas.trap: Using modified duration for a callable, or squaring the shift; the denominator has 2 x Delta Curve, not (Delta Curve)^2.

formulas.name: Effective convexity
formulas.vars: PV_-, PV_+ = values after parallel benchmark curve shifts down and up by Delta Curve (decimal), holding OAS constant
formulas.use: Measures curvature of the price-yield relation; callables near the call price show negative effective convexity.
formulas.trap: Dividing by 2 x Delta Curve as in duration; convexity squares the shift, and a negative result is normal for callables.

formulas.name: One-sided durations
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} D_{\text{down}} = \frac{PV_{-} - PV_0}{\Delta\text{Curve} \times PV_0} \\ D_{\text{up}} = \frac{PV_0 - PV_{+}}{\Delta\text{Curve} \times PV_0} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: D_down = sensitivity to a rate decline; D_up = sensitivity to a rate rise; Delta Curve = size of the one-way shift
formulas.use: Measures rate-fall and rate-rise sensitivity separately when an embedded option makes the price response asymmetric.
formulas.trap: Callables have the smaller duration for rate declines (call caps gains); putables have the smaller duration for rate rises.

formulas.name: Capped and floored floaters
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} V_{\text{capped}} = V_{\text{straight}} - V_{\text{cap}} \\ V_{\text{floored}} = V_{\text{straight}} + V_{\text{floor}} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: V_straight = value of the same floater with no cap or floor (par at each reset with a zero margin)
formulas.use: Values floaters with coupon limits: the cap is an issuer option that lowers value, the floor an investor option that adds it.
formulas.trap: Reversing the signs; a cap limits the coupon the investor receives, so it is subtracted, while a floor protects the investor.

formulas.name: Conversion value and minimum value
formulas.vars: CR = conversion ratio (shares per bond); S_0 = current share price; V_straight = value as an otherwise identical straight bond
formulas.use: Conversion value is what the shares received are worth now; a convertible should not trade below the higher of CV and straight value.
formulas.trap: Taking conversion value as the floor when straight value is higher; the minimum value is the larger of the two.

formulas.name: Conversion price and market conversion price
formulas.vars: P_cb = market price of the convertible bond; CR = conversion ratio
formulas.use: Conversion price is fixed at issue; market conversion price is the effective cost per share when buying the bond today.
formulas.trap: Dividing par by CR when the question asks what a buyer pays per share today; that needs the bond's market price.

formulas.name: Convertible premium ratio and premium over straight
formulas.vars: MCP = market conversion price = P_cb / CR; MCP - S_0 = market conversion premium per share
formulas.use: The premium ratio prices the embedded stock call per share; premium over straight value measures downside if the stock collapses.
formulas.trap: Dividing the per-share premium by MCP instead of the current share price; the premium ratio uses S_0 as its base.

formulas.name: Convertible bond value components
formulas.vars: C_stock = investor's call on the shares (conversion option); C_issuer = issuer's call on the bond; P_investor = bondholder's put, if any
formulas.use: Decomposes a callable, putable convertible into a straight bond plus the conversion option, less the issuer call, plus the put.
formulas.trap: Adding the issuer call; it belongs to the issuer, lowers value and can force conversion, capping the investor's upside.

formulas.name: Expected price change from credit migration
formulas.vars: p_i = one-year transition probability to rating i; Delta s_i = spread change for that migration; expected return = YTM + E(%Delta P)
formulas.use: Adjusts a credit bond's YTM for expected rating changes from a transition matrix to estimate its expected return.
formulas.trap: Treating YTM as the expected return; downgrades are likelier and widen spreads more, so E(%Delta P) is negative even without default.

formulas.name: Expected exposure and loss given default
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} EE_t = \sum_{j} p_j\,V_{j,t} + C_t \\ LGD_t = EE_t \times (1 - RR) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: V_{j,t} = no-default bond value at node j on date t; p_j = node probability; C_t = coupon due at t; RR = recovery rate
formulas.use: Gives the amount at risk on each date (probability-weighted value plus coupon) and the loss if default happens then.
formulas.trap: Using the time-0 value or par as the exposure on every date; exposure changes over time as the bond rolls toward par.

formulas.name: Probability of default from a hazard rate
formulas.vars: h = constant hazard rate (default probability in a year given survival to its start); (1 - h)^t = survival probability
formulas.use: Converts a conditional hazard rate into each year's unconditional default probability and the cumulative POD for CVA.
formulas.trap: Using h as the POD for every year or summing hazard rates; later-year PODs shrink because the issuer must survive first.

formulas.name: Credit valuation adjustment (CVA)
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} CVA = \sum_{t} LGD_t \times POD_t \times DF_t \\ FV = VND - CVA \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: POD_t = unconditional risk-neutral POD for year t; DF_t = risk-free discount factor; VND = value assuming no default
formulas.use: Values credit risk as the PV of expected losses; the default-free value less CVA is the fair value of the risky bond.
formulas.trap: Discounting expected losses at the risky yield, which double-counts credit risk; CVA uses risk-free discount factors.

formulas.name: Credit spread approximation (credit triangle)
formulas.vars: POD = annual default probability; LGD = loss as a share of exposure; h = hazard rate; RR = recovery rate
formulas.use: Quick link between default probability, loss severity and annual spread; also backs out a hazard rate from a CDS spread.
formulas.trap: Quoting CVA as the spread; CVA is a price amount per 100 of par, while the credit spread is an annual yield premium.

formulas.name: Risk-neutral probability of default
formulas.vars: pi = risk-neutral one-period POD; RR = recovery rate; r = risk-free rate; P_0 = price per 100 face of a one-period risky zero
formulas.use: Backs out the market-implied default probability from a risky bond price; these PODs are the inputs for pricing and CVA.
formulas.trap: Ignoring recovery, which understates pi, or reading pi as a real-world forecast; it exceeds historical default rates.

formulas.name: Structural (Merton) model
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} D_0 = PV(K) - \text{Put}(A_0, K) \\ E_0 = \text{Call}(A_0, K) = A_0 - D_0 \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: A_0 = value of firm assets; K = face value of zero-coupon debt due at T; options are European options on the firm's assets
formulas.use: Treats equity as a call on firm assets and risky debt as riskless debt less a put; default occurs if assets end below K.
formulas.trap: Swapping the options: debt holders are short the put on the assets, while equity holders are long the call.

formulas.name: Tranche loss in securitized debt
formulas.vars: L = collateral pool loss; A = tranche attachment point; D = detachment point (all in the same units, e.g., % of the pool)
formulas.use: Allocates pool losses to a tranche: nothing until losses pass the attachment point, then capped at the tranche width D - A.
formulas.trap: Forgetting the cap at D - A or charging senior tranches first; losses hit the most junior tranche first.

formulas.name: CDS payout on a credit event
formulas.vars: RR = recovery set by the auction price of the cheapest-to-deliver obligation (% of par); n = names in an equally weighted index
formulas.use: Gives the protection seller's payment after a credit event; in an index CDS each default pays on 1/n of the notional.
formulas.trap: Paying full notional without recovery, or the whole index notional for one default; the index notional then falls by 1/n.

formulas.name: CDS upfront payment and price
formulas.vars: S = market CDS spread; FC = standard fixed coupon (1% investment grade, 5% high yield in North America); EffSpreadDur = CDS spread duration
formulas.use: Settles at inception the PV gap between the market spread and the standard coupon; the buyer pays when the spread exceeds it.
formulas.trap: Getting the sign wrong: if the spread is below the fixed coupon, the upfront is negative and the seller pays the buyer.

formulas.name: CDS upfront from protection and premium legs
formulas.vars: protection leg = sum of DF x POD x LGD; premium leg = sum of DF x survival probability x fixed coupon (per 1 of notional)
formulas.use: Values a CDS exactly from hazard-rate expected payoffs; a positive result means the protection buyer pays upfront.
formulas.trap: Weighting premium payments by POD instead of survival probability; the buyer stops paying the coupon after default.

formulas.name: Change in CDS value from a spread change
formulas.vars: Delta S = change in the CDS spread (decimal); the seller's change in value is the mirror image
formulas.use: Marks a CDS to market after spreads move; a long/short trade nets this across legs, such as one name vs the index.
formulas.trap: Thinking the protection buyer profits only on default; the buyer gains whenever spreads widen, and the seller loses that amount.

formulas.name: Duration-neutral CDS curve trade
formulas.vars: N = notional of each leg; D = effective spread duration of the short-tenor and long-tenor CDS
formulas.use: Sizes a steepener (buy long-tenor, sell short-tenor protection) so parallel spread moves roughly cancel.
formulas.trap: Using equal notionals, which leaves a large parallel-spread bet; selling long-tenor protection is a flattener, not a steepener.

definitions.term: Par, spot and forward curve ordering
definitions.def: With an upward-sloping spot curve, forward rates lie above spot rates and spot rates above par rates (f > z > par); a downward-sloping curve reverses the order, and a flat curve makes all three equal.
If future spot rates equal today's forwards, every maturity earns the same one-period return. Realized spots below the forwards make longer bonds outperform; above the forwards, they underperform.
Unbiased expectations: forward = expected future spot. Liquidity preference adds a positive term premium. Segmented markets and preferred habitat let supply and demand by maturity drive yields.
TED spread = 3-month market reference rate minus the 3-month T-bill yield; MRR-OIS spread = reference rate minus the overnight indexed swap rate. Both widen when bank credit and funding stress rise.
Law of one price: identical cash flows must sell at one price. Dominance arbitrage buys the cheaper of two same-risk, same-timing assets; value additivity says a bond equals the sum of its strips.
A rate tree is calibrated when it prices every benchmark par bond at par, making it arbitrage-free. Check: a plain floater paying the node rate is worth par at every node of a calibrated tree.

definitions.term: Volatility and curve shape vs option value
definitions.def: Higher rate volatility raises both call and put values, lowering callable and raising putable prices. An upward-sloping curve makes an embedded call less valuable and a put more valuable than a flat curve.

Structural (Merton) models derive default from asset value falling below debt, using option pricing. Reduced-form models treat default as a random event with a hazard rate driven by observable variables.

Spread at each maturity = risky spot rate minus benchmark spot rate. High-quality issuers usually show upward-sloping spread curves; distressed issuers show flat or inverted curves as near-term default risk dominates.
Scores rank individuals and small firms; ratings rank corporate, sovereign and structured debt. Both are ordinal rankings, not default probabilities, and through-the-cycle ratings lag market spreads.

Credit events: bankruptcy, failure to pay and, outside standard North American contracts, restructuring. A downgrade is not one. A succession event such as a merger or spin-off can split the CDS among successors.
Basis = CDS spread minus the bond's credit spread over the same benchmark. A negative basis means the bond is cheap versus protection: buy the bond and buy CDS protection to capture the gap.

distractors: Implied forward rate from spot rates
Par rate (swap rate) from discount factors
Arbitrage-free bond value from spot rates
drill.why: A ratio of two discount factors, longer over shorter, is the forward price of a zero delivered at A. The implied forward rate uses compounded spot rates and a root, not discount factors alone.

distractors: Bootstrapping spot rates from par rates
Arbitrage-free bond value from spot rates
drill.why: One minus the last discount factor over the annuity of all discount factors is the coupon that prices a bond at par, i.e., the swap rate. Bootstrapping solves the same par condition for z_n, not for the coupon.

distractors: Arbitrage-free bond value from spot rates
drill.why: One constant spread added to each benchmark spot rate in a fixed cash-flow discount is the Z-spread. OAS is added to the one-period rates of a tree with option exercise rules, not to spot rates.

Down-shift value minus up-shift value over 2 x shift x PV_0 is effective duration. Effective convexity adds both shocked values, subtracts 2PV_0 and squares the shift; one-sided durations use a single shift.
Summing both shocked values, subtracting 2PV_0 and dividing by the squared shift measures curvature: effective convexity. Effective duration takes the difference of the shocked values over 2 x shift.

distractors: Option-free bond value at a tree node
drill.why: Multiplying the lower node rate by e^{2 sigma root t} gives the adjacent higher rate in a lognormal tree. The node-value formula discounts cash flows; Ho-Lee and KWF are continuous-time short-rate models, not node spacings.

distractors: Expected price change from credit migration
drill.why: Summing exposures to each key-rate change estimates the percentage price change from a non-parallel shift. Credit migration also sums -ModDur x Delta s, but weights spread changes by transition probabilities.

distractors: Expected exposure and loss given default
CDS upfront from protection and premium legs
drill.why: Discounted LGD x POD summed over dates is the CVA, a price amount. The credit triangle is an annual spread with no discounting; the CDS protection leg looks similar but is netted against the premium leg.

distractors: Probability of default from a hazard rate
Expected price change from credit migration
drill.why: Pricing a risky zero as the discounted payoff weighted by survival (100) and default (RR x 100) solves for the risk-neutral POD. The hazard-rate formula converts a conditional rate, not a bond price.

distractors: Change in CDS value from a spread change
CDS upfront from protection and premium legs
drill.why: Market spread minus the standard fixed coupon, times spread duration, is the upfront at inception. The mark-to-market formula uses the change in spread after trade date, not the gap to the fixed coupon.

distractors: CDS payout on a credit event
drill.why: A spread change times spread duration times notional is the buyer's mark-to-market gain or loss. The upfront uses spread minus the fixed coupon; the payout uses 1 - RR and applies only after a credit event.

formulas.name: Forward price, cost-of-carry model
formulas.vars: CC = carrying costs (storage, insurance); CB = carry benefits (dividends, coupons, convenience yield); r = annual risk-free rate
formulas.use: General no-arbitrage forward price: finance the spot purchase, add the PV of costs, subtract the PV of benefits, carry to T.
formulas.trap: Adding benefits instead of subtracting them; the spot holder, not the forward long, receives dividends and coupons.

formulas.name: Equity forward price with discrete dividends
formulas.vars: D_i = dividend paid at time t_i before the forward expires; r = annual risk-free rate; T = years to expiration
formulas.use: Prices a forward on a stock that pays known dividends before expiry by removing their present value from spot.
formulas.trap: Subtracting undiscounted dividends from spot, or including dividends paid after the forward expires.

formulas.name: Equity index forward, continuous dividend yield
formulas.vars: r_c = continuously compounded risk-free rate; delta = continuously compounded dividend yield on the index
formulas.use: Prices index forwards and futures when dividends are modeled as a continuous yield on the index.
formulas.trap: Plugging an annually compounded rate into the exponent, or adding the dividend yield; dividends lower the forward price.

formulas.name: Equity forward value during its life
formulas.vars: PV_t(D) = PV of dividends still to be paid before expiry; equivalent form: V_t = (F_t - F_0)/(1+r)^{T-t}
formulas.use: Values a long equity forward before expiry: spot minus PV of remaining dividends minus PV of the locked-in price.
formulas.trap: Discounting F_0 over the original term T instead of the remaining T - t, or ignoring dividends still to be paid.

formulas.name: Futures value between daily settlements
formulas.vars: F_{t-1} = last settlement price; the gain or loss is paid as variation margin at each daily settlement
formulas.use: Values a futures position between daily settlements; after settlement the gain is paid and the value resets to zero.
formulas.trap: Confusing futures price with value: after daily settlement the price may be far from F_0 but the contract's value is zero.

formulas.name: FRA rate (implied forward MRR)
formulas.vars: r_S, d_S = rate and days to FRA expiration; r_L, d_L = rate and days to the end of the loan (3x6: d_S = 90, d_L = 180)
formulas.use: Gives the fixed rate that makes an FRA worth zero at initiation: the implied forward rate for the underlying loan period.
formulas.trap: Annualizing with 360/d_L instead of 360/(d_L - d_S), or reading 3x6 as a 6-month loan; it is 3 months starting in 3 months.

formulas.name: FRA settlement payment (long, pay-fixed)
formulas.vars: MRR = market reference rate set at FRA expiration; days = days in the underlying loan period; NA = notional amount
formulas.use: Cash paid at FRA expiration (advanced set, advanced settled); the long receives when the reference rate exceeds the FRA rate.
formulas.trap: Not discounting at the realized MRR; the interest difference belongs to the end of the loan period but is settled at its start.

formulas.name: FRA value during its life
formulas.latex: V_g = \frac{(FRA_g - FRA_0) \times t_m \times NA}{1 + r_{T} \times t_{T}}
formulas.vars: FRA_g = today's FRA rate for the same loan period; t_m = loan period (days/360); r_T, t_T = current rate and time to the loan's end
formulas.use: Marks an existing long FRA to market: today's FRA rate minus the contract rate, discounted from the loan's end date.
formulas.trap: Discounting only to the FRA expiration date; the interest difference accrues at the end of the underlying loan period.

formulas.name: Bond futures quoted price (conversion factor)
formulas.vars: S_0 + AI_0 = full price of the cheapest-to-deliver bond; AI_T = accrued interest at delivery; FVCI = FV of coupons received; CF = conversion factor
formulas.use: Gives the no-arbitrage quoted futures price; at delivery the short receives QFP x CF + accrued interest.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to divide by CF or to subtract accrued interest at delivery; bond futures are quoted clean and per standardized bond.

formulas.name: Interest rate futures hedge size
formulas.vars: BPV = value change per 1 bp; for a USD 1M 3-month SOFR contract BPV_fut = USD 25; futures price = 100 - rate in percent
formulas.use: Sizes a hedge of a future borrowing or lending rate with 3-month reference-rate futures.
formulas.trap: Buying futures to hedge rising borrowing costs; the price is 100 minus the rate, so a borrower sells futures.

formulas.name: Currency forward price (covered interest parity)
formulas.vars: f/d = units of price currency f per 1 unit of base currency d; r_f = rate of the price currency; r_d = rate of the base currency
formulas.use: Prices a currency forward from spot and the two interest rates; the higher-rate currency trades at a forward discount.
formulas.trap: Inverting the rate ratio; the price currency's rate goes in the numerator, matching the f/d quote.

formulas.name: Currency forward value during its life
formulas.vars: F_t = today's forward rate for the remaining term (from covered interest parity); value is in the price currency
formulas.use: Values a long base-currency forward mid-life: new forward minus contract rate, times notional, discounted in price currency.
formulas.trap: Discounting at the base-currency rate, or using today's spot instead of today's forward rate for the remaining term.

formulas.name: Swap fixed rate from discount factors
formulas.vars: PV_i(1) = discount factor for payment date i; FS_0 is per period, so annualize by multiplying by payments per year
formulas.use: Sets the fixed rate that gives a new interest rate or equity swap zero value: the par rate on the discount curve.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to annualize: with quarterly payments the formula returns a quarterly rate that must be multiplied by 4.

formulas.name: Interest rate swap value during its life
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} V = (FS_t - FS_0) \times \sum_{i} PV_i(1) \times NA \\ V = NA \left[1 - \left(FS_0 \sum_{i} PV_i(1) + PV_n(1)\right)\right] \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: V = value to the pay-fixed side; FS_0, FS_t = original and current periodic swap rates (annual rate x accrual period); line 2 holds on a reset date (floater = par)
formulas.use: Values a pay-fixed swap as the rate gap times the remaining annuity, or as a par floater minus a fixed-rate bond.
formulas.trap: Giving the gain to the fixed receiver; rising rates help the fixed payer. Sum only the remaining discount factors.

formulas.name: Currency swap value
formulas.latex: V = B_{d}(\text{receive leg}) - S_t \times B_{f}(\text{pay leg})
formulas.vars: B = value of each leg as a fixed-rate bond including final notional, on its own currency's current curve; S_t = today's spot (d per f)
formulas.use: Values a fixed-for-fixed currency swap by pricing each leg as a bond and converting the foreign leg at today's spot rate.
formulas.trap: Converting at the initial exchange rate, or leaving out the final notional exchange when pricing each leg.

formulas.name: Equity swap value (receive equity, pay fixed)
formulas.vars: S_{t-1} = equity level at the last reset; PV_i(1) = discount factors for the remaining fixed payment dates
formulas.use: Values an equity swap between resets: notional grown by the equity return since reset, minus the fixed-rate bond.
formulas.trap: Valuing the equity leg at par between resets; it is NA x S_t / S_{t-1}, and a negative return is paid by the equity receiver.

formulas.name: One-period binomial value (risk-neutral)
formulas.vars: u, d = up and down gross returns on the underlying; pi = risk-neutral probability of the up move; V+, V- = option payoffs
formulas.use: Prices an option as its risk-neutral expected payoff discounted at the risk-free rate.
formulas.trap: Using real-world probabilities or the stock's expected return; pi depends only on u, d and r.

formulas.name: Binomial hedge ratio and replication
formulas.vars: h = shares per option in the riskless hedge; c+, c- and S+, S- = option and stock values after the up and down moves
formulas.use: Gives the shares per call that make long stock plus short call riskless; the call equals hS_0 minus the PV of that payoff.
formulas.trap: Inverting the ratio (stock range over option range); h is the option's value spread over the stock's and is negative for puts.

formulas.name: Two-period binomial option value
formulas.vars: c++, c+-, c-- = terminal payoffs after two up, one up and one down, and two down moves; pi = risk-neutral up probability
formulas.use: Prices a European option over two steps directly from terminal payoffs weighted by risk-neutral path probabilities.
formulas.trap: Counting the middle node once; two paths reach it, hence 2 pi (1 - pi). American options need a node-by-node exercise check.

formulas.name: American put value at a tree node
formulas.vars: X - S_node = exercise (intrinsic) value; the second term = discounted risk-neutral continuation value
formulas.use: Values an American put by backward induction, exercising early wherever intrinsic value beats continuation value.
formulas.trap: Pricing an American put with the European two-period formula; early exercise can pay even on a non-dividend stock.

formulas.name: Put-call parity and put-call-forward parity
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} c_0 + \frac{X}{(1+r)^T} = p_0 + S_0 \\ c_0 - p_0 = \frac{F_0 - X}{(1+r)^T} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: c_0, p_0 = European call and put with the same strike X and expiry T; F_0 = forward price for T
formulas.use: Links European calls, puts, the underlying and bonds or forwards; a violation signals a conversion or reversal arbitrage.
formulas.trap: Applying parity to American options, or using an undiscounted strike; X and F_0 - X are discounted at the risk-free rate.

formulas.name: BSM d1 and d2
formulas.vars: r = continuously compounded risk-free rate; sigma = annual volatility of the underlying's returns; T = years to expiration
formulas.use: Inputs to BSM: N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability a call finishes in the money; N(d1) is the call delta.
formulas.trap: Adding sigma root T for d2, or using a simple annual rate; with a dividend yield, r becomes r - delta in d1.

formulas.name: Black-Scholes-Merton call and put
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} c_0 = S_0N(d_1) - Xe^{-rT}N(d_2) \\ p_0 = Xe^{-rT}N(-d_2) - S_0N(-d_1) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: N(.) = standard normal cumulative probability; N(-d) = 1 - N(d); no dividends on the underlying
formulas.use: Values European options on a non-dividend stock: PV of expected share delivery minus PV of expected strike payment.
formulas.trap: Using N(d1) and N(d2) in the put; the put needs N(-d2) and N(-d1), with the strike term first.

formulas.name: BSM with continuous dividend yield
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} c_0 = S_0e^{-\delta T}N(d_1) - Xe^{-rT}N(d_2) \\ p_0 = Xe^{-rT}N(-d_2) - S_0e^{-\delta T}N(-d_1) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: delta = continuous dividend yield (foreign risk-free rate for currency options); d1 = [ln(S_0/X) + (r - delta + sigma^2/2)T] / (sigma root T)
formulas.use: Values options on dividend-paying stocks, indexes or currencies by replacing S_0 with S_0 e^{-delta T}.
formulas.trap: Leaving delta out of d1; a higher yield lowers call values and raises put values through both S_0 e^{-delta T} and d1.

formulas.name: Black model for options on futures
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} c_0 = e^{-rT}\left[F_0N(d_1) - XN(d_2)\right] \\ p_0 = e^{-rT}\left[XN(-d_2) - F_0N(-d_1)\right] \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: F_0 = futures price; d1 = [ln(F_0/X) + (sigma^2/2)T] / (sigma root T); d2 = d1 - sigma root T
formulas.use: Values European options on futures or forwards; the whole bracket is discounted because the futures price embeds carry.
formulas.trap: Adding r to d1 as in BSM; Black's d1 has only sigma^2/2, because the futures price already embeds the cost of carry.

formulas.name: Payer and receiver swaptions (Black model)
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} PAY = NA \cdot AP\sum_{j} PV_{0,t_j}(1)\left[FS\,N(d_1) - X\,N(d_2)\right] \\ REC = NA \cdot AP\sum_{j} PV_{0,t_j}(1)\left[X\,N(-d_2) - FS\,N(-d_1)\right] \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: AP = accrual period (1/payments per year); FS = forward swap rate; X = exercise rate; PV_{0,t_j}(1) = discount factors of the swap dates
formulas.use: Values the right to pay fixed (payer, a call on the swap rate) or receive fixed (receiver, a put) in a future swap.
formulas.trap: Mixing up names: a payer swaption gains when rates rise. Omitting the annuity factor leaves a rate, not a value.

formulas.name: Option delta (BSM)
formulas.vars: delta = dividend yield (0 for a non-dividend stock); call delta lies between 0 and 1, put delta between -1 and 0
formulas.use: Measures the option value change for a small change in the underlying price; the base for delta hedging.
formulas.trap: Using N(d2) for delta; N(d2) is the risk-neutral exercise probability, while delta uses N(d1).

formulas.name: Delta hedge: number of options or shares
formulas.vars: Delta_H = delta of one hedging unit (an option's delta, or 1 for a share); negative N_H = sell. Short N_c calls: buy N_c x Delta_c shares
formulas.use: Gives the number of hedging options or shares that brings a portfolio's delta to zero.
formulas.trap: Setting the hedge once and leaving it; delta moves with price and time (gamma), so the hedge must be rebalanced.

formulas.name: Delta-gamma approximation of option price change
formulas.vars: Delta = option delta; Gamma = change in delta per 1 change in the underlying; Delta S = change in the underlying price
formulas.use: Estimates the option price change for a move in the underlying, correcting delta's linear estimate for curvature.
formulas.trap: Dropping the 1/2 or the gamma term; for a long option, delta alone understates gains and overstates losses on large moves.

formulas.name: Theta and gamma-theta break-even
formulas.vars: Theta = value change as one period of time passes, all else equal; Delta S = move per period that offsets the time decay
formulas.use: Measures time decay; a delta-hedged long-gamma position profits only when moves exceed the break-even Delta S.
formulas.trap: Calling theta always negative; deep in-the-money European puts can have positive theta.

formulas.name: Vega and value change from volatility
formulas.vars: nu = vega, value change per 1 percentage point change in volatility; Delta sigma = change in volatility in the same units
formulas.use: Estimates option value change when implied volatility moves; long calls and long puts both have positive vega.
formulas.trap: Mixing units of vega and Delta sigma; and vega is largest for at-the-money options, not deep in- or out-of-the-money ones.

formulas.name: Rho of calls and puts
formulas.vars: rho = value change per unit change in the continuously compounded risk-free rate; spot options on a non-dividend stock
formulas.use: Measures option sensitivity to the risk-free rate: calls gain and puts lose when rates rise.
formulas.trap: Carrying the signs to futures options; in the Black model a higher r lowers both call and put values through discounting.

definitions.def: If the market forward exceeds S_0(1 + r)^T, cash-and-carry (buy spot, borrow, sell forward) earns the difference at expiry; if it is below, reverse cash-and-carry (short spot, lend, buy forward) does.
Daily settlement makes futures and forward prices differ only when rates and the underlying are correlated: positive correlation makes futures more valuable (higher price), negative correlation less.

The deliverable bond cheapest for the short: the highest implied repo rate, usually also the lowest basis (clean price minus futures price x conversion factor). Conversion factors equalize bonds only imperfectly.

Current exposure = max(V, 0): only the side with positive mark-to-market value is exposed to the other's default. Collateral, netting and clearing reduce it; currency swaps carry more (principal is re-exchanged).

Early exercise of an American call on a non-dividend stock is never optimal, so it equals the European call. American puts, and calls just before a large dividend, can be worth more than European ones.
The underlying follows geometric Brownian motion (lognormal prices) with constant volatility and risk-free rate, frictionless continuous trading, no arbitrage and European exercise.
The volatility that makes the BSM or Black model price equal the market price. It is the market's forward-looking estimate, unlike historical volatility measured from past returns.

Implied volatility varies by strike (smile or skew; low-strike equity puts are usually pricier) and by expiry (term structure). The surface plots both; a flat surface would mean BSM's constant sigma held.

distractors: Equity forward price with discrete dividends
Equity index forward, continuous dividend yield
Equity forward value during its life
drill.why: Spot plus PV of carrying costs minus PV of benefits, compounded to T, is the general cost-of-carry forward price. The discrete-dividend version is the special case with only dividends; forward value subtracts a discounted F_0.

distractors: Equity forward price with discrete dividends
Currency forward value during its life
drill.why: Current spot net of remaining dividends minus the locked-in price discounted over T - t is a forward's value mid-life. The forward price compounds spot to T; futures value is just the price change since the last settlement.

distractors: Swap fixed rate from discount factors
drill.why: The ratio of long-period to short-period growth, annualized over the gap d_L - d_S, is the implied forward rate an FRA locks in. Settlement and value both multiply a rate difference by notional and discount it.

distractors: Currency forward value during its life
Equity index forward, continuous dividend yield
drill.why: Spot times the ratio of price-currency to base-currency growth is covered interest parity. Currency forward value instead takes F_t - F_0 times notional and discounts it at the price-currency rate.

distractors: Interest rate swap value during its life
Equity swap value (receive equity, pay fixed)
drill.why: One minus the final discount factor over the sum of discount factors is the par (fixed) swap rate. Swap value multiplies a rate difference by that annuity; the FRA rate compares two simple-interest growth factors.

distractors: Delta hedge: number of options or shares
drill.why: Option payoff spread over stock price spread in a binomial step is the hedge ratio h. BSM delta is the continuous-time analog N(d1); the delta-hedge count divides portfolio delta by an instrument's delta.

The whole bracket of futures price and strike discounted at e^{-rT} is the Black call on a futures. BSM discounts only the strike; the swaption uses the forward swap rate and an annuity factor, not e^{-rT}.
N(d1), adjusted for dividend yield, and N(d1) - 1 for puts are option deltas. Rho uses N(d2) times T X e^{-rT}; the binomial hedge ratio is a discrete payoff spread, not a normal probability.

distractors: Vega and value change from volatility
drill.why: Delta times the move plus half gamma times the squared move estimates an option's price change. The theta break-even uses the same gamma term but sets it equal to time decay instead of adding a delta term.

formulas.name: Commodity futures total return
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} R_{TR} = R_{price} + R_{roll} + R_{coll} + R_{rebal} \\ R_{ER} = R_{TR} - R_{coll} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: R_coll = T-bill return on collateral backing the full notional; R_rebal = return from resetting index weights (multi-commodity index only); ER = excess-return index
formulas.use: Splits a fully collateralized commodity futures position or index return into price, roll, collateral and rebalance sources.
formulas.trap: Treating the spot price change as the investor's return, or comparing an excess-return index with a total-return index; the gap is the T-bill yield.

formulas.name: Roll return
formulas.vars: F_near = expiring contract price sold; F_far = longer-dated contract price bought
formulas.use: Measures the gain or loss on a long position from rolling into the next contract: negative in contango, positive in backwardation.
formulas.trap: Dividing by the far price, or flipping the sign: in contango the far contract is dearer, so rolling a long position loses even if spot is flat.

formulas.name: Theory of storage futures price
formulas.vars: One-year horizon; r = financing rate; U = storage cost in dollars; Y = convenience yield in dollars (benefit of holding the physical good)
formulas.use: Prices a futures contract at full carry less convenience yield; a quote above it invites cash-and-carry arbitrage (buy spot, store, sell futures).
formulas.trap: Adding the convenience yield instead of subtracting it; Y lowers the futures price, which is why tight inventories push the curve into backwardation.

formulas.name: Implied convenience yield
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} F_0 = S_0\,e^{(r + c - y)T} \\ y = r + c - \frac{\ln(F_0/S_0)}{T} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Continuous rates: r = financing rate; c = storage cost rate; y = convenience yield rate; T = years to expiry
formulas.use: Backs out the convenience yield the market prices from spot and futures; a high y signals scarce inventories and positive roll for longs.
formulas.trap: Mixing dollar storage costs with continuous rates, or assuming contango means zero convenience yield; y can be large yet below r + c.

formulas.name: Commodity total return swap net payment
formulas.vars: N = notional; R_index = index return over the reset period; r_T-bill + s = floating leg for the same period (annual rate scaled to the period)
formulas.use: Gives the investor's net settlement on a swap that replicates a commodity index without trading or rolling futures.
formulas.trap: Applying the annual floating rate to a monthly reset, or treating swap exposure as free; the floating leg offsets the yield on idle collateral.

formulas.name: Unsmoothed real estate return
formulas.vars: R* = reported appraisal-based return; a = smoothing parameter (first-order autocorrelation); R_t = estimated true return
formulas.use: Removes appraisal lag from a private real estate index before its volatility and correlation feed an asset allocation model.
formulas.trap: Using raw appraisal returns in mean-variance optimization; smoothed volatility and correlation are too low, so private real estate is over-allocated.

formulas.name: Net operating income (NOI)
formulas.vars: PGI = potential gross income at full occupancy; bracket = effective gross income (EGI); OpEx = taxes, insurance, maintenance, utilities, management
formulas.use: Measures the property's unlevered operating income, the input to direct capitalization, DCF and NAV.
formulas.trap: Deducting mortgage interest, depreciation or income taxes; NOI is before financing and taxes, so those deductions understate value.

formulas.name: Direct capitalization value and cap rate
formulas.vars: NOI_1 = next year's NOI; r = required return (discount rate); g = constant NOI growth; cap rate also observed from comparable sales
formulas.use: Values a stabilized property in one step from next year's NOI; a higher cap rate means a lower value.
formulas.trap: Capitalizing trailing NOI at a forward cap rate, or treating the cap rate as the discount rate; they differ by expected growth g.

formulas.name: Property DCF value with terminal cap rate
formulas.vars: r = discount rate; R_exit = terminal (going-out) cap rate applied to year n+1 NOI; selling costs, if given, reduce the terminal value
formulas.use: Values a property with uneven NOI (lease-up, rent steps, vacancies) and an assumed sale at the end of the holding period.
formulas.trap: Capitalizing year n NOI instead of year n+1, or using an exit cap rate below the going-in rate for an older building without justification.

formulas.name: Cost approach value
formulas.vars: Depreciation = physical deterioration + functional obsolescence + external (locational or economic) obsolescence; land is not depreciated
formulas.use: Values new or special-purpose property with few comparables; it caps value because a buyer could build instead.
formulas.trap: Depreciating the land, or using reproduction cost of an exact replica instead of replacement cost of a building with equal utility.

formulas.name: Real estate operating leverage
formulas.vars: Second form holds when operating expenses are fixed (gross lease); under a triple-net lease expenses pass through and DOL is close to 1
formulas.use: Shows how sharply NOI moves for a change in rental income; compares gross-lease and net-lease property risk.
formulas.trap: Comparing NOI margins without checking lease type; a gross lease leaves fixed costs and expense inflation with the landlord.

formulas.name: Levered equity return
formulas.vars: r_A = unlevered asset return (property yield, or mortgage asset yield for a mortgage REIT); r_D = cost of debt; D/E = debt-to-equity
formulas.use: Shows how mortgage debt changes a property owner's equity return, and how a mortgage REIT's spread is magnified by leverage.
formulas.trap: Assuming leverage always helps: once r_A falls below r_D each extra unit of debt lowers r_E, and a value decline hits equity by a multiple.

formulas.name: Debt service coverage and loan-to-value ratios
formulas.vars: Debt service = annual interest plus scheduled principal on the mortgage
formulas.use: Lender tests that cap how much can be borrowed against a property; the lower of the two implied loan sizes is the maximum loan.
formulas.trap: Counting interest only as debt service on an amortizing loan, or sizing the loan on LTV alone when the DSCR limit binds first.

formulas.name: Equity dividend rate (cash-on-cash return)
formulas.vars: Equity invested = purchase price minus loan amount; uses first-year figures
formulas.use: Measures the first-year levered cash yield on the investor's equity in a financed property purchase.
formulas.trap: Treating it as a total return; it ignores appreciation, principal paydown and sale proceeds, which only a levered IRR captures.

formulas.name: Funds from operations (FFO)
formulas.latex: FFO = NI + D\&A_{RE} - \text{Gains on sales} + \text{Losses on sales}
formulas.vars: D&A_RE = real estate depreciation and amortization; deferred tax charges are also added back; NAREIT adds back property impairments
formulas.use: Converts REIT net income into the standard recurring earnings measure by removing real estate depreciation and sale results.
formulas.trap: Adding back gains on property sales; gains are subtracted and losses added back because property sales are not recurring operations.

formulas.name: Adjusted funds from operations (AFFO)
formulas.vars: Straight-line rent adj. = non-cash rent booked above cash received; recurring capex includes leasing commissions and tenant improvements
formulas.use: Approximates cash available for dividends, the better base for payout analysis and P/AFFO valuation.
formulas.trap: Treating FFO as free cash flow; FFO ignores recurring capex, and AFFO is not standardized, so check capex assumptions before comparing.

formulas.name: P/FFO and P/AFFO relative valuation
formulas.vars: ps = per share; peer = sector or comparable-REIT average multiple, ideally on forecast figures
formulas.use: Values REIT shares by applying a peer multiple to forecast FFO or AFFO per share.
formulas.trap: Applying a P/FFO multiple to AFFO (or the reverse); the same REIT trades at a higher P/AFFO because AFFO is smaller than FFO.

formulas.name: REIT net asset value per share (NAVPS)
formulas.vars: NOI_1 = next year's cash NOI (straight-line rent removed, trailing NOI grown); other assets = cash, receivables, land; goodwill excluded
formulas.use: Estimates private-market value per REIT share, the benchmark for judging whether the share price is rich or cheap.
formulas.trap: Using balance-sheet book value or capitalizing trailing NOI at a forward cap rate; intangibles such as goodwill are excluded from NAV.

formulas.name: Premium (discount) to NAVPS
formulas.vars: Solving for the cap rate that makes NAVPS equal the share price gives the market-implied cap rate
formulas.use: Compares the public share price with estimated private-market value and reveals the cap rate the market is pricing in.
formulas.trap: Buying every discount as a bargain; it often prices in cap-rate increases that lagging appraisal-based NAV has not yet shown.

formulas.name: Conditional linear factor model
formulas.vars: D_t = 1 in crisis periods, 0 otherwise; normal-period exposure = beta_k, crisis exposure = beta_k + gamma_k
formulas.use: Evaluates a hedge fund strategy's factor exposures separately in normal and stress periods to test whether diversification holds.
formulas.trap: Reading beta_k alone as the crisis exposure; it is beta_k + gamma_k, and a positive equity gamma means diversification fails in sell-offs.

formulas.name: Merger arbitrage spread
formulas.vars: ER = exchange ratio (acquirer shares per target share); in a cash deal, spread = offer price - target price
formulas.use: Measures the gain locked in by buying the target and shorting ER acquirer shares if a stock-for-stock deal closes.
formulas.trap: Calling the trade market neutral; deal breaks cluster in equity sell-offs, so the payoff resembles a short put on deal completion.

formulas.name: Convertible arbitrage delta hedge
formulas.vars: Delta = sensitivity of the convertible's value to the share price; conversion ratio = shares received per bond
formulas.use: Sizes the short stock position that neutralizes the equity exposure of a long convertible bond.
formulas.trap: Shorting the full conversion ratio instead of delta times it, or never rebalancing; the hedge must be reset as delta changes.

definitions.def: Contango: longer-dated futures trade above near-dated (or spot), so rolling longs loses. Backwardation: longer-dated futures trade below, so rolling longs gains.
Keynes: producers hedge by selling futures, so F0 sits below the expected future spot price and long speculators earn a premium. It compares futures with expected spot, not today's spot.
Adds consumers who hedge by buying futures. If producer shorts dominate, F0 < E(S_T) and longs earn the premium; if consumer longs dominate, F0 > E(S_T) and shorts earn it.
Commodities hedge unexpected, not expected, inflation; the link is strongest for energy and industrial metals, so an energy-heavy index has a higher inflation beta than a diversified one.
Equity vs debt crossed with private vs public: direct property, private loans, REITs and REOCs, and MBS or CMBS. Public quadrants give liquidity; private give control but are illiquid.
Core: stabilized, low-leverage, income-driven. Value-add: re-leasing or renovation with moderate leverage. Opportunistic: development or distress, high leverage, return mostly at exit.
A US REIT must hold mostly real estate assets, earn mostly real estate income and distribute at least 90% of taxable income (not FFO), so growth is funded by new equity or debt.
Holds mortgages or MBS funded with short-term repo and earns a leveraged spread. Little depreciable property, so it is valued on price-to-book and dividend yield, not P/FFO.
Equity-related, event-driven, relative value, opportunistic (global macro, managed futures), specialist and multi-manager. The group signals dominant risk, leverage, liquidity and crisis behavior.
Gross = (long + short)/capital measures leverage; net = (long - short)/capital measures directional market exposure. Holding shorts does not make a fund market neutral; net beta does.
CTAs go long assets in uptrends and short those in downtrends, sized to a volatility target. Positively skewed returns that help in long bear markets but suffer in sharp V-shaped reversals.
Expected return = (expected recovery - purchase price)/purchase price, driven by the Chapter 11 or Chapter 7 outcome. Illiquid, model-marked positions understate volatility and need long lockups.
A lockup bars (hard) or penalizes (soft) early redemptions; notice periods and gates cap withdrawals. Terms should match asset liquidity, or a crisis forces fire sales or suspensions.

distractors: Commodity total return swap net payment
drill.why: Near minus far over the near price is the gain from selling the expiring contract and buying the next one: roll return. Total return adds price, collateral and rebalance return on top of roll; convenience yield comes from spot vs futures.

distractors: Commodity total return swap net payment
drill.why: Spot financed for a year plus dollar storage minus dollar convenience yield is the theory-of-storage futures price. The implied convenience yield row solves the continuous version for y; it does not output a futures price.

distractors: Property DCF value with terminal cap rate
REIT net asset value per share (NAVPS)
Debt service coverage and loan-to-value ratios
drill.why: Next year's NOI over a cap rate equal to r - g values a stabilized property in one step: direct capitalization. The DCF row discounts each year's NOI plus an exit value; NAVPS adds other assets, subtracts liabilities and divides by shares.

distractors: Debt service coverage and loan-to-value ratios
Direct capitalization value and cap rate
drill.why: Cash flow after debt service divided by the equity put in is the first-year cash-on-cash yield, the equity dividend rate. DSCR divides NOI by debt service; the levered equity return formula uses r_A, r_D and D/E, not cash flows.

distractors: REIT net asset value per share (NAVPS)
drill.why: Starting from FFO and deducting non-cash rent and recurring capex gives AFFO, the cash-based measure. FFO itself starts from net income and adds back real estate depreciation; NAVPS capitalizes NOI instead.

distractors: Direct capitalization value and cap rate
drill.why: Capitalized NOI plus other assets minus liabilities, per share, is the REIT's NAVPS. Direct capitalization stops at NOI over the cap rate for one property; the premium compares price with NAVPS once it is known.

formulas.name: Real default-free rate from the IMRS
formulas.vars: m_1 = inter-temporal rate of substitution (marginal utility of consumption next period / today); P_0 = price of a real default-free zero paying 1
formulas.use: Prices a default-free inflation-indexed zero and gives the real risk-free rate implied by investors' consumption preferences.
formulas.trap: Thinking more uncertainty raises real rates; it raises precautionary saving and E(m), which lifts bond prices and lowers the real rate.

formulas.name: Risky asset price with payoff covariance
formulas.vars: R = real default-free rate; cov(P1, m1) = covariance of the payoff with the IMRS (negative for procyclical assets)
formulas.use: Shows why assets that pay off poorly in bad times trade below their risk-free discounted value and carry a risk premium.
formulas.trap: Equating risk premium with volatility; a volatile asset that pays off in recessions has positive covariance and a low or negative premium.

formulas.name: Long yield, expected short rates and term premium
formulas.vars: Bar = average expected short rate over the bond's life; pi = term premium for inflation and real-rate uncertainty
formulas.use: Splits a default-free long yield into expected policy rates and a term premium when reading the slope of the nominal curve.
formulas.trap: Reading the slope as a pure rate forecast; pi is high when inflation shocks dominate and can be near zero or negative when growth shocks dominate.

formulas.name: Break-even inflation
formulas.vars: y_real = yield on an inflation-linked bond of the same maturity; theta = expected inflation; pi = inflation risk premium
formulas.use: Extracts market-implied inflation from nominal and inflation-linked government yields of the same maturity.
formulas.trap: Treating BEI as a clean inflation forecast; it includes the risk premium pi, and linker illiquidity biases it the other way.

formulas.name: Credit spread components
formulas.vars: PD = probability of default; LGD = loss given default; the premium compensates for defaults clustering in recessions
formulas.use: Explains why credit spreads exceed expected loss and widen countercyclically, far more for high yield than for AA bonds.
formulas.trap: Treating the spread as pure expected loss; spreads exceed historical PD x LGD because defaults cluster when marginal utility is high.

formulas.name: Required return build-up: equity and real estate
formulas.vars: l = real rate; theta = expected inflation; pi = inflation premium; gamma = credit premium; kappa = equity premium; phi = illiquidity premium
formulas.use: Builds required returns from default-free real rate upward; commercial real estate adds an illiquidity premium to the equity-like return.
formulas.trap: Assuming kappa is stable; the equity premium is countercyclical, so a recession cuts expected earnings and raises the discount rate together.

formulas.name: Taylor rule policy rate
formulas.vars: r_n = neutral real rate; pi = current inflation; pi* = target inflation; (Y - Y*) = output gap in percent
formulas.use: Benchmarks the central bank's short rate; a policy rate below i* signals easy policy and a steeper curve.
formulas.trap: Dropping the current inflation term, which leaves a real rate, or plugging the neutral real rate r_n in as if it were the nominal policy rate.

formulas.name: Active return from active weights
formulas.vars: Delta w_i = portfolio weight minus benchmark weight; overweights are funded by underweights
formulas.use: Computes active return versus a fully invested benchmark from active weights and security returns.
formulas.trap: Subtracting the risk-free rate or using portfolio weights instead of active weights; active return is measured against the benchmark.

formulas.name: Value added: allocation and selection
formulas.vars: j = asset class; first sum = asset allocation (active class weights x benchmark class returns); second = selection within each class
formulas.use: Splits a multi-asset portfolio's value added into asset-allocation and security-selection components.
formulas.trap: Crediting a positive total to security selection; allocation can mask negative selection, and the two pieces often have opposite signs.

formulas.name: Information ratio (ex post)
formulas.vars: Denominator = active risk (tracking error), the standard deviation of active returns
formulas.use: Measures realized active return per unit of active risk; the manager input that matters when combining with the benchmark.
formulas.trap: Calling all active return alpha; with beta not equal to 1, part of it is a beta bet that alpha divided by residual risk would strip out.

formulas.name: Sharpe ratio of benchmark plus active portfolio
formulas.vars: Holds at the optimal active risk level, with active returns uncorrelated with the benchmark
formulas.use: Gives the highest Sharpe ratio achievable by combining the benchmark with an active manager; pick the manager with the highest IR.
formulas.trap: Adding the ratios (0.40 + 0.30 = 0.70); the squares add, so SR_P = 0.50 and the manager lifts the Sharpe ratio by only 0.10.

formulas.name: Optimal active risk and active fund weight
formulas.vars: sigma_B = benchmark total volatility; sigma_A = the fund's own active risk; rest of the portfolio is held in the benchmark
formulas.use: Sizes active risk to maximize the total Sharpe ratio, then sets the weight on the active fund versus the benchmark.
formulas.trap: Inverting the ratio (SR_B/IR) or plugging in the fund's total volatility instead of the benchmark's volatility sigma_B.

formulas.name: Fundamental law of active management
formulas.vars: TC = transfer coefficient (0 to 1); IC = ex ante risk-weighted forecast correlation; BR = independent bets per year
formulas.use: Links skill, breadth and constraints to the expected information ratio and expected active return.
formulas.trap: Using BR instead of its square root, or counting holdings as breadth when many bets come from one common view.

formulas.name: Market-timing information coefficient
formulas.vars: % correct = hit rate on binary up or down calls; breadth = number of independent calls per year
formulas.use: Converts a market timer's hit rate into an IC for the fundamental law; 55% correct gives IC = 0.10.
formulas.trap: Using the hit rate (0.55) itself as the IC, or treating monthly calls from one slow macro view as independent breadth.

formulas.name: Constrained optimal active risk and Sharpe ratio
formulas.vars: IR* = unconstrained information ratio; TC < 1 under long-only, sector or turnover constraints
formulas.use: Sizes active risk and the achievable Sharpe ratio for a constrained (for example long-only) manager.
formulas.trap: Sizing a long-only fund with the unconstrained IR*; that overstates optimal tracking error and expected active return by 1/TC.

formulas.name: ETF premium or discount to NAV
formulas.vars: NAV = end-of-day net asset value; iNAV = intraday indicative value updated during trading
formulas.use: Measures how far the ETF price departs from the value of its holdings; positive is a premium.
formulas.trap: Reading a premium on a foreign-equity or bond ETF as mispricing; the NAV is often stale and the ETF price is the better estimate.

formulas.name: Authorized participant arbitrage profit
formulas.vars: Costs = creation or redemption fees plus trading costs on the basket and the ETF shares
formulas.use: Shows when APs create units (ETF at a premium) or redeem them (ETF at a discount), keeping price within a cost band of NAV.
formulas.trap: Thinking investor buying creates ETF shares; only APs create or redeem, and only when the gap exceeds their all-in costs.

formulas.name: Tracking difference and tracking error
formulas.vars: TD is a level (usually about minus the expense ratio); TE is the standard deviation of periodic differences
formulas.use: Separates an ETF's cost of tracking (tracking difference) from how variable the gap to the index is (tracking error).
formulas.trap: Treating tracking error as the cost of ownership; a fund with near-zero TE can still lag the index every year by its TD.

formulas.name: ETF total holding-period cost
formulas.vars: Bid-ask spread = full spread (half on entry, half on exit); ER = annual expense ratio; T = holding period in years; add premium paid, less discount
formulas.use: Ranks ETFs on the same index for a given horizon: spreads dominate short holds, expense ratios dominate long holds.
formulas.trap: Ranking ETFs on expense ratio alone; for a 3-month tactical trade the spread can cost more than years of fee difference.

formulas.name: Leveraged ETF multi-period return
formulas.vars: r_t = daily index return; exposure resets daily, so the return compounds the leveraged daily returns
formulas.use: Computes a daily-reset leveraged or inverse ETF's return over several days and shows volatility drag.
formulas.trap: Expecting twice the index return over months; in a volatile, trendless market a 2x ETF can lose while the index is flat.

formulas.name: Arbitrage pricing theory (APT) expected return
formulas.vars: lambda_j = risk premium of factor j (expected excess return of a pure factor portfolio); solve K + 1 portfolios for R_F and the lambdas
formulas.use: Prices well-diversified portfolios from factor sensitivities and premiums, or backs out R_F and the lambdas from given portfolios.
formulas.trap: Assuming APT needs the market portfolio or names the factors; it only rules out arbitrage, and factors and premiums are estimated.

formulas.name: Macroeconomic factor model return
formulas.vars: F = factor surprise (actual minus expected); b = sensitivity estimated by time-series regression; epsilon = firm-specific surprise
