formulas.use: Computes a stock's realized return from macro surprises and firm-specific news.
formulas.trap: Plugging in the actual level of GDP growth or inflation instead of the surprise; expected values are already in E(R_i).

formulas.name: Fundamental factor standardized exposure
formulas.vars: x_ik = company attribute (book-to-market, size, momentum); mean and sigma are cross-sectional across the universe
formulas.use: Turns a company attribute into a factor exposure in a fundamental model; factor returns are then estimated cross-sectionally.
formulas.trap: Mixing up the model types: fundamental models observe exposures and estimate factor returns; macro models do the reverse.

formulas.name: Portfolio variance from a factor model
formulas.vars: b = vector of portfolio factor exposures; Sigma_F = factor covariance matrix; sigma_epsilon squared = specific (residual) variance
formulas.use: Decomposes portfolio risk into systematic factor risk and specific risk to see which exposures drive volatility.
formulas.trap: Ignoring the off-diagonal factor covariances, or adding factor and specific standard deviations instead of variances.

formulas.name: Active return: factor tilts and selection
formulas.vars: beta_P,k - beta_B,k = active exposure to factor k; F_k = realized factor return; asset selection is the residual
formulas.use: Attributes active return to deliberate or accidental factor tilts versus security selection.
formulas.trap: Crediting all outperformance to stock picking; a persistent size or value tilt earns factor return a cheap passive product delivers.

formulas.name: Active factor risk and active specific risk
formulas.vars: Active factor risk comes from active factor exposures; active specific risk from security-level active weights and residual variances
formulas.use: Shows whether a manager's active risk comes from style and sector bets or from genuine stock-specific positions.
formulas.trap: Adding the standard deviations (3% + 4% = 7%); the components add only as variances, giving active risk of 5%.

formulas.name: Pure factor portfolio weights
formulas.vars: Exposure 1 to the target factor and 0 to every other; a risk-free asset (exposures 0) can absorb the remaining weight
formulas.use: Builds a portfolio that isolates one factor, to hedge that exposure or to bet on one factor view alone.
formulas.trap: Omitting the zero condition on the other factors or the budget constraint, so the pure inflation bet still carries GDP risk.

formulas.name: Tracking portfolio condition
formulas.latex: \sum_i w_i b_{i,k} = b_{B,k} \quad \text{for every factor } k
formulas.vars: b_B,k = the target's (benchmark's) sensitivity to factor k; weights also sum to 1
formulas.use: Builds a portfolio that copies a benchmark's full factor profile, so active return comes only from selection.
formulas.trap: Confusing it with a factor portfolio: a factor portfolio targets (1, 0, 0), a tracking portfolio copies the target's whole vector.

formulas.name: Parametric (variance-covariance) VaR
formulas.vars: z = 1.65 at 5%, 2.33 at 1%; for T periods scale mu by T and sigma by the square root of T; daily mu often set to 0
formulas.use: Computes VaR assuming normal returns from portfolio mean, volatility (weights, volatilities, correlations) and value.
formulas.trap: Scaling the mean by the square root of T or sigma by T, or using z = 1.65 for a 1% VaR; horizon and confidence must match.

formulas.name: Historical and Monte Carlo simulation VaR
formulas.vars: Q = alpha-percentile of simulated P/L; historical: current positions repriced with past market moves; Monte Carlo: draws from assumed distributions
formulas.use: Reads VaR from the simulated P/L distribution, capturing fat tails and option non-linearity that parametric VaR misses.
formulas.trap: Using the portfolio's own past returns instead of today's positions repriced under past moves, or trusting more draws to cure model risk.

formulas.name: Conditional VaR (expected shortfall)
formulas.vars: Under simulation, average only the losses beyond the VaR cut-off; CVaR is at least as large as VaR at the same level
formulas.use: Measures the average size of tail losses that VaR ignores; sub-additive, so it never penalizes diversification.
formulas.trap: Averaging all losses instead of only the tail, or assuming equal VaR means equal tail risk; CVaR can differ widely.

formulas.name: Incremental VaR
formulas.vars: Marginal VaR = change in VaR per small change in a position's size; incremental VaR is the full change from adding or removing the position
formulas.use: Measures how adding, removing or resizing a position changes total portfolio VaR, capturing diversification.
formulas.trap: Ranking positions by standalone VaR; a high-VaR position that hedges the book can have low or negative incremental VaR.

formulas.name: Relative VaR from ex ante tracking error
formulas.vars: TE ex ante = forecast standard deviation of portfolio minus benchmark returns from current active weights
formulas.use: Measures a benchmarked manager's risk of underperforming the benchmark rather than of losing money outright.
formulas.trap: Reporting absolute VaR to a benchmarked client; it mostly reflects market risk the client chose, not the manager's active bets.

formulas.name: Surplus at risk
formulas.vars: A = asset value; L = liability value (for example a pension's PBO); risk is on the surplus A - L
formulas.use: Measures a pension fund's or insurer's risk on assets minus liabilities, the relevant risk for liability-driven investors.
formulas.trap: Judging a pension on asset-only VaR; short-duration bonds look safe but raise surplus risk against long-duration liabilities.

formulas.name: Duration and convexity price sensitivity
formulas.vars: Delta y in decimals (0.01 = 100 bp); assumes a parallel shift; use effective duration and convexity for callables and MBS
formulas.use: Estimates a bond portfolio's price change for a yield shock as a sensitivity measure alongside VaR.
formulas.trap: Entering Delta y as 1 instead of 0.01, or subtracting the convexity term when yields fall; positive convexity adds both ways.

formulas.name: Backtest return net of trading costs
formulas.latex: R_{net} \approx R_{gross} - \text{Round trips per year} \times \text{Cost per round trip}
formulas.vars: Cost per round trip includes commissions, spread and market impact; add borrow fees for the short side
formulas.use: Converts a gross backtest return into a realistic live estimate for a strategy's turnover.
formulas.trap: Assuming one cost level for all strategies; high-turnover and small-cap strategies pay far more, often erasing the gross edge.

formulas.name: Probability of a false discovery in multiple tests
formulas.vars: alpha = significance level per test; n = number of independent strategy variants tested
formulas.use: Shows how data snooping inflates apparent significance and why a higher t-statistic hurdle (about 3) is used.
formulas.trap: Reporting the best variant's t-statistic without disclosing how many variants were tried; 50 tests at 5% give about a 92% false-hit chance.

definitions.term: Yield curve slope over the cycle
definitions.def: Term spread = 10-year minus 3-month yield. Steep at troughs (low policy rates, expected hikes), flat or inverted near peaks; an inversion has preceded recessions but is not a timing tool.
When growth shocks dominate, bonds rally as stocks fall (negative correlation). When inflation shocks dominate, both fall together, as in 2022, and bonds lose their hedge value.
Ex ante risk-weighted correlation between forecast and realized active returns. Even skilled managers have small ICs, often about 0.05 to 0.10, so a high IR needs breadth.

definitions.term: Ex post active return and noise
definitions.def: Realized R_A = TC x IC_R x sqrt(BR) x sigma_A + noise. Forecasts explain TC squared of active-return variance, so a constrained skilled manager can still lag for years.
Mixing a portfolio with cash leaves the Sharpe ratio unchanged; mixing an active fund with its benchmark leaves the IR unchanged. Adding cash to an active fund changes its IR.
Market makers price in creation and redemption fees, the basket's own spreads, hedging risk and profit. ETF liquidity comes mainly from its holdings, not its screen volume.

definitions.term: Fundamental vs macro vs statistical models
definitions.def: Macro: observed factor surprises, sensitivities estimated by time series. Fundamental: observed attributes, factor returns estimated cross-sectionally. Statistical: factors extracted from covariance.
If a diversified portfolio sits off the APT line, buy the cheap side and short a replica with identical factor exposures and zero net investment; the return difference is riskless.
The minimum loss expected over a horizon with a given probability, P(Loss > VaR) = alpha. It is not the worst case, ignores tail size and is not sub-additive in general.

definitions.term: Scenario analysis and reverse stress test
definitions.def: Scenario analysis replays historical or hypothetical shocks on current holdings without a probability. A reverse stress test finds the shocks that would cause an unacceptable loss.
Allocating total risk (VaR or tracking error) to desks or managers. Uncorrelated sleeves add in variance, total = sqrt(sum of squares), so linear addition wastes the budget.
Look-ahead uses data not yet released at the decision date, such as restated figures. Survivorship drops delisted firms. Point-in-time data with reporting lags removes both.
A rolling window estimates on past data, holds out of sample, then rolls forward once through history. Bootstrapping or Monte Carlo instead builds a distribution of many simulated paths.

distractors: Optimal active risk and active fund weight
Constrained optimal active risk and Sharpe ratio
drill.why: The squares of the benchmark Sharpe ratio and the IR add, so the root gives the Sharpe ratio of the combined portfolio. The constrained version multiplies IR* by TC; optimal active risk is a ratio times sigma_B, not a square root.

distractors: Sharpe ratio of benchmark plus active portfolio
Constrained optimal active risk and Sharpe ratio
drill.why: IR over the benchmark Sharpe ratio, times benchmark volatility, is the active risk that maximizes the total Sharpe ratio. The constrained version has a TC multiplier; the ex post IR divides active return by tracking error.

distractors: Sharpe ratio of benchmark plus active portfolio
drill.why: Transfer coefficient times skill times the square root of breadth is the fundamental law's expected IR. The ex post IR is measured from realized returns and tracking error; the timing IC is only the skill input.

distractors: Probability of a false discovery in multiple tests
drill.why: Twice the hit rate minus one maps a 50% coin-flip to zero skill and 100% to one: the market timer's IC. It feeds the fundamental law but is not the IR; the false-discovery formula uses a significance level, not a hit rate.

distractors: Active return: factor tilts and selection
Active factor risk and active specific risk
drill.why: Two sums by asset class, active class weights times benchmark class returns plus portfolio weights times within-class active returns, give allocation plus selection. Factor attribution uses active betas times factor returns instead.

distractors: ETF premium or discount to NAV
Relative VaR from ex ante tracking error
drill.why: The return gap to the index and its standard deviation are tracking difference and tracking error. A premium compares price with NAV, not returns; relative VaR scales a forecast tracking error by z and portfolio value.

distractors: Relative VaR from ex ante tracking error
Historical and Monte Carlo simulation VaR
drill.why: z times portfolio volatility less the expected return, times portfolio value, is parametric VaR on total returns. Relative VaR uses tracking error and surplus at risk uses the volatility of assets minus liabilities.

distractors: Historical and Monte Carlo simulation VaR
drill.why: An expected loss conditional on exceeding VaR is the average tail loss, conditional VaR. Simulation VaR reads a single percentile; incremental VaR is the change in total VaR from a position.

distractors: Active return: factor tilts and selection
drill.why: Unit exposure to one factor and zero to the rest defines a pure factor portfolio. A tracking portfolio instead sets every exposure equal to the benchmark's, which is rarely the vector (1, 0).

distractors: Long yield, expected short rates and term premium
Real default-free rate from the IMRS
drill.why: Nominal minus real yield of the same maturity leaves expected inflation plus the inflation risk premium: break-even inflation. The term premium compares long yields with expected short rates, not with linkers.

code: Act with integrity, competence, diligence, respect, and in an ethical manner toward the public, clients, prospects, employers, colleagues, and other market participants.
Place the integrity of the investment profession and the interests of clients above your own personal interests.
Use reasonable care and exercise independent professional judgment in investment analysis, recommendations, actions, and other professional activities.
Practice, and encourage others to practice, in a professional and ethical manner that reflects credit on yourself and the profession.
Promote the integrity and viability of the global capital markets for the ultimate benefit of society.
Maintain and improve your professional competence, and strive to maintain and improve the competence of other investment professionals.

standards.name: Knowledge of the Law
standards.requires: Follow the stricter of the law that actually governs the activity and the Code and Standards. Do not knowingly join or assist a violation: raise it with a supervisor or compliance, then dissociate, and in extreme cases resign.
standards.trap: Raising a firm's overbilling once and then continuing to process the invoices is still participation. Dissociation is required; reporting to regulators is not.

standards.name: Independence and Objectivity
standards.requires: Use reasonable care to keep independence and objectivity against issuer, banking, sales, and client pressure. Pay your own travel, limit issuer gifts, and accept issuer-paid research only for a flat, pre-agreed, disclosed fee.
standards.trap: Softening a sell to a hold, or delaying the report, after an issuer threatens to cut access is still a breach. A fee rising with a positive rating is never acceptable.

standards.name: Misrepresentation
standards.requires: Make no knowing misrepresentation, including by omission, about analysis, recommendations, performance, services, or credentials. Credit others' work even when paraphrased, and never guarantee returns on risky investments.
standards.trap: Calling a volatile bond fund 'guaranteed 7%' because it has earned 7%, or recoloring a rival's chart uncredited. Only recognized statistical-service data needs no credit.

standards.name: Misconduct
standards.requires: Do not engage in professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit, or commit any act that reflects adversely on your professional reputation, integrity, or competence, such as padding expense reports.
standards.trap: Labeling every lie I(D): false claims to clients about performance or credentials are I(C). A medical bankruptcy or civil disobedience is not misconduct by itself.

standards.name: Material Nonpublic Information
standards.requires: If you possess material nonpublic information, do not act or cause others to act on it. Inform compliance so the issuer goes on a watch or restricted list, urge public disclosure, and wait until it is disseminated.
standards.trap: Treating a CFO's remark to six analysts on a private call as public, or tipping a PM 'in confidence' without trading. Mosaic theory fails if any one input is MNPI.

standards.name: Market Manipulation
standards.requires: Do not distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with intent to mislead market participants, whether transaction-based (wash trades, marking the close) or information-based (spreading false rumors).
standards.trap: Excusing quarter-end buying of thin holdings to lift reported NAV because the trades were real and paid for. Intent to mislead decides it; tax-loss selling is fine.

standards.name: Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
standards.requires: Act for clients' benefit, ahead of employer and self. Identify the true client (plan beneficiaries, not the sponsor), use commissions only for research that helps them, vote proxies under a written policy, and seek best execution.
standards.trap: Filing soft-dollar furniture or a costlier share class picked for firm revenue under III(B) or III(C). Both are III(A) loyalty breaches that put the firm first.

standards.name: Fair Dealing
standards.requires: Deal fairly and objectively with all clients when disseminating recommendations, changing them, or taking action. Send changes to all clients near-simultaneously and allocate oversubscribed issues pro rata by a disclosed method.
standards.trap: Allocating a hot IPO by client size or order of calls, or letting a premium tier get rating changes first. Disclosed service tiers are fine; earlier changes are not.

standards.name: Suitability
standards.requires: Learn each client's objectives and constraints, keep a written IPS and review it at least annually and after major life events, and judge suitability for the total portfolio. Manage pooled funds to the stated mandate.
standards.trap: Testing a fund's trades against investors' IPSs: a fund is judged on its mandate, so style drift breaches III(C). Keeping a growth mix after retirement also breaches it.

standards.name: Performance Presentation
standards.requires: Make reasonable efforts to keep performance fair, accurate, and complete: include terminated accounts, state gross or net of fees, label simulated results, and disclose that a record was earned at a prior firm.
standards.trap: Defending a pitch book because every number shown is accurate. Dropping terminated losing accounts or passing off a prior-firm record as the new firm's breaches III(D).

standards.name: Preservation of Confidentiality
standards.requires: Keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential unless it concerns illegal client activity, disclosure is required by law, or the client permits it. Cooperating with the PCP is allowed.
standards.trap: Thinking confidentiality blocks a lawful regulator request or a PCP inquiry; both are allowed. A journalist gets nothing, and the duty survives account closure.

standards.name: Loyalty
standards.requires: Act for your employer's benefit and do not harm it. You may prepare to leave on your own time, but do not solicit clients or take client lists, models, or records before departure. Get consent for competing independent practice.
standards.trap: Taking the client list she built, or soliciting clients before resigning. After leaving she may contact them from memory or public data unless a non-compete applies.

standards.name: Additional Compensation Arrangements
standards.requires: Do not accept gifts, benefits, or compensation that compete with or might conflict with your employer's interest unless you first obtain written consent from all parties involved, disclosing terms, amount, and duration.
standards.trap: Accepting a client's performance bonus or a paid board seat on verbal approval, or telling the employer after payment. Written consent (email counts) must come first.

standards.name: Responsibilities of Supervisors
standards.requires: Make reasonable efforts so supervisees, members or not, comply with laws, rules, and the Code and Standards. On a suspected breach, promptly investigate and limit their activity; refuse the role in writing if compliance is weak.
standards.trap: Reporting a front-running trader upward and accepting his promise to stop. The supervisor must investigate and restrict or monitor his trading while the review runs.

standards.name: Diligence and Reasonable Basis
standards.requires: Exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness, and have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by research, for every recommendation. Review third-party research, understand quantitative models, and vet external managers.
standards.trap: Defending a buy based on an unverified social-media rumor because it proved true; V(A) judges the basis at the time. A dissenter on a sound group report may stay on it.

standards.name: Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
standards.requires: Disclose the investment process's basic format and principles, its significant risks and limitations, and any material change promptly. Judge which factors matter and separate fact from opinion.
standards.trap: Switching to a quant screen and adding futures without telling clients because the fund name and benchmark are unchanged; material process changes need prompt notice.

standards.name: Record Retention
standards.requires: Develop and keep records that support investment analysis, recommendations, actions, and client communications. Records belong to the employer; absent a regulatory period, CFA Institute recommends at least seven years.
standards.trap: Deleting research notes after a year, or taking her models to a new employer. Records are the firm's; she recreates support from public data. Seven years is a fallback.

standards.name: Disclosure of Conflicts
standards.requires: Make full, fair, and prominent disclosure to employer, clients, and prospects of anything that could reasonably impair independence and objectivity: beneficial ownership, family ties, board seats, banking ties.
standards.trap: Relying on one boilerplate line or disclosing only to compliance. Name the real conflict, such as her 4,000 shares; disclosure does not permit trading ahead of clients.

standards.name: Priority of Transactions
standards.requires: Clients first, then employer, then trades in which you are a beneficial owner. Follow pre-clearance and blackout rules; a family member's fee-paying account is treated like any other client account.
standards.trap: Buying for herself an hour before a client block, or always filling her parents' fee-paying account last. Only accounts she beneficially owns go to the back of the queue.

standards.name: Referral Fees
standards.requires: Disclose to your employer, clients, and prospects, before the engagement begins, any compensation or benefit received from or paid to others for recommending products or services, with its nature and estimated value.
standards.trap: Disclosing a fund provider's 0.25% trailing payment only to the employer, vaguely, or after the client signs. Nature and estimated value come before the engagement.

standards.name: Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
standards.requires: Do not compromise the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute, the CFA designation, or its exams: no cheating, no disclosing questions, topics, or formulas tested, and no misrepresenting information to CFA Institute.
standards.trap: Posting after the exam which broad topics or formulas appeared heavily. That breaches VII(A) without quoting any question; opinions on difficulty or policy are fine.

standards.name: Reference to CFA Institute, CFA Designation, and CFA Program
standards.requires: Do not misrepresent or exaggerate CFA membership, the designation, or candidacy. Use CFA as an adjective, keep membership current (dues plus the annual conduct statement), and never imply a partial designation.
standards.trap: Writing 'CFA Level II' or 'CFA (expected 2027)', or a 'CFA-certified' process. Say 'Level II candidate in the CFA Program' while registered, or 'passed Level I'.

definitions.term: Applying the Standards to a case
definitions.def: Isolate each fact, ask what it compromised (law, objectivity, truth, client, employer, markets), cite the specific Standard, then pick the action it requires. Code principles alone are rarely the answer.

Refusing to take part in a violation: object to a supervisor or compliance, stop the work, remove your name from documents, and resign in extreme cases. Silence while continuing counts as participation.
Ratings must reflect the analyst's own work, free of issuer, banking, sales, or client pressure. Firms separate research from banking, shield negative ratings, and disclose deal ties.
Allowed only for a flat fee agreed before writing, unrelated to the conclusion or share price, with full analyst control and clear disclosure. Payment in shares or warrants compromises independence.

A modest gift from a client for past service falls under I(B): disclose it to the employer, before accepting if possible. Pay tied to future performance is IV(B) compensation and needs prior written consent.
Management giving material information to a subset of analysts or investors. It stays nonpublic until disseminated to the market at large, for example by press release or regulatory filing.
Combining public information with nonmaterial nonpublic pieces, such as supplier channel checks, to reach a material conclusion is permitted. It fails if any single input is MNPI. Keep the records.

definitions.term: Firewall, watch list and restricted list
definitions.def: A firewall logs and controls wall crossings. A watch list is a confidential list of issuers where the firm holds MNPI; a restricted list openly halts trading and recommendations in the name.
Research paid for with client brokerage commissions. Commissions are client assets, so they may buy only research that helps those clients; furniture or rent paid this way breaches III(A).
For a separately managed client, suitability is tested against the IPS for the whole portfolio. For a pooled fund it is tested against the stated mandate, so style drift breaches III(C).
Proxies are client assets voted in the client's interest under a written, disclosed policy. A documented cost-benefit analysis can justify not voting routine or share-blocking proxies.

definitions.term: GIPS vs the Code and Standards
definitions.def: GIPS is a voluntary, firm-wide performance standard with no partial compliance. It helps satisfy III(D), which does not require it, and never replaces individual duties under the other Standards.

Prior written agreement from all parties, in practice the employer, to outside compensation that could conflict with the employer's interest, stating its nature, amount, and duration. Email qualifies.

Before relying on outside research or a quant model, review its assumptions, rigor, timeliness and objectivity, and understand its parameters and limits. Unreviewed reliance breaches V(A) if the basis is unsound.

A window around client trades or rating changes in which staff may not trade the security personally. With pre-clearance and holdings reports it enforces VI(B) priority without banning personal trading.

The PCP may close a case, issue a cautionary letter, or propose private or public censure, suspension, or charter revocation. Candidates are bound from registration and can be barred from the CFA Program.
